pages.title: Dinosaur Coloring Book Prompts for Kids & KDP
pages.metaDescription: Dinosaur coloring page prompts for five 24-page books, page by page: baby dinos, dino jobs, a fossil dig, prehistoric eras and adult patterns.
pages.intro: Dinosaurs are one of the steadiest sellers in kids' coloring on Amazon KDP and Etsy, because every generation of children goes through a dinosaur phase. Here are five dinosaur coloring books of 24 pages each, written out page by page: baby dinosaurs at home for toddlers, dinosaurs with jobs and sports, a fossil dig and museum trip, a realistic prehistoric world by era, and intricate patterned dinosaurs for adults. Copy one page at a time into ChatGPT, Gemini or any AI image tool, or copy all 24 and make the whole book.
tips: Keep the toddler book about one big dinosaur doing one familiar thing per page; parents of 2-5 year olds buy recognisable routines, not roaring predators.
Mix famous species (T-rex, triceratops, stegosaurus) with lesser-known ones like therizinosaurus and pachycephalosaurus so the Look Inside preview shows real variety.
The fossil-dig and museum angle pairs well with museum gift shops and school trips, so list it with paleontology keywords as well as dinosaur ones.

prompts.name: Baby dinosaurs' day at home
prompts.brief: 24 pages of chubby baby dinosaurs living a little kid's day at home, from hatching in the morning to sleeping at night: a T-rex brushing its teeth, a triceratops eating cereal, a stegosaurus in a bubble bath with a rubber duck, a brachiosaurus jumping in puddles, an ankylosaurus building a block tower, a pterodactyl flying a kite, a birthday party, a picnic, a blanket fort and a T-rex asleep with its teddy bear.
prompts.why: Parents and grandparents of preschoolers buy cozy dinosaur books as gifts, and a familiar daily routine on every page keeps small kids coloring to the end.

pages.title: Farm Animal Coloring Book Prompts: Cute Barnyard Pages
pages.metaDescription: Farm animal coloring page prompts for five 24-page books, page by page: baby animals, named animals, farm seasons, a county fair and farmhouse art.
pages.intro: Farm animals are often the very first animals a toddler learns to name, which makes a farm animal coloring book a perfect first coloring book and a dependable KDP seller. Here are five farm coloring books of 24 pages each, written out page by page: baby barnyard animals for toddlers, 24 farm animals and breeds with their names, a year of seasons on the farm, a day at the county fair, and patterned farmhouse animals for adults. Copy one page at a time into ChatGPT, Gemini or any AI image tool, or copy all 24 and make the whole book.
keywords: farm animal coloring pages for toddlers
tips: Baby animals (chicks, piglets, lambs, calves) outsell adult farm animals for the under-5 crowd; lead the cover and first pages with them.
A named-animal book with one animal per page doubles as a first-words book, so you can list it under early learning as well as coloring.
Seasonal farm scenes like spring lambing, pumpkin harvest and a snowy barn let one farm book rank for several gift seasons.

pages.title: Ocean Animal Coloring Book Prompts: Sea Creatures & Coral Reefs
pages.metaDescription: Ocean animal coloring book prompts for five 24-page books, written page by page: toddler sea friends, tide pools, sharks, the deep sea and ocean mandalas.
pages.intro: Sea creatures work for every age, from a toddler's first smiling whale to an adult colorist's intricate jellyfish mandala, and teachers use them for ocean units. These ocean animal coloring book prompts cover five 24-page books: sea friends for toddlers, tide pools and beach life, sharks and ocean giants, the deep sea, and an under the sea mandala collection. Each book is written out page by page, so you can paste one page at a time into ChatGPT, Gemini or any AI image tool.
keywords: ocean mandala coloring book for adults
deep sea coloring pages for kids
tips: Give each ocean book its own zone (beach, open ocean, deep sea, reef) so five books share a theme but almost no pages.
Sharks and whales are a strong sub-niche with boys aged 6-10; name real species like hammerhead and whale shark in the listing.
Summer and beach-vacation keywords lift ocean books from May to August, so publish ahead of the season.

pages.intro: Unicorn coloring books are a perennial best seller on Amazon KDP, especially as birthday and holiday gifts for kids aged 4 to 10. Here are five unicorn coloring books of 24 pages each, written out page by page: baby unicorns on clouds for toddlers, unicorns at parties and hobbies, a kingdom of magical creatures, an enchanted forest quest for tweens, and ornate unicorn mandalas for teens and adults. Copy one page at a time into ChatGPT, Gemini or any AI image tool, or copy all 24 and make the whole book.
tips: Plain unicorn books are crowded on KDP; a magical creatures book with pegasus, griffins and fairies widens the keywords you can rank for.
Give every page an activity (a tea party, a carousel, a sleepover) so the unicorns are doing something, not just standing in a field.
An enchanted-quest book with a young hero gives older kids a story to follow and stands apart from the toddler-heavy unicorn shelf.

pages.title: Dragon Coloring Book Prompts for Kids, Teens & Adults
pages.metaDescription: Dragon coloring book prompts for five 24-page books, page by page: silly baby dragons, elemental dragons, dragon riders, Eastern dragons and adult art.
pages.intro: Dragons sit at the crossroads of fantasy and adventure, so a dragon coloring book appeals to boys and girls alike and keeps selling to teens and adults too. Here are five dragon coloring books of 24 pages each: silly baby dragons for little kids, a different dragon for every element, a dragon riders' academy for tweens, flowing Eastern dragons and festivals, and an intricate collection for adult colorists. Each book is written out page by page, so you can paste one page at a time into ChatGPT, Gemini or any AI image tool, or copy all 24 and make the whole book.
tips: For under-6s, make dragons silly instead of fierce: tiny puffs of fire, wobbly first flights and toasted marshmallows keep the book gift-friendly.
An elemental book (fire, ice, forest, storm, crystal) means a 24-page book never repeats the same dragon in a new pose.

pages.title: Jungle & Safari Animal Coloring Book Prompts
pages.metaDescription: Jungle safari coloring prompts for five 24-page books, page by page: baby animals, a jungle explorer trip, rainforest layers, the savanna and mandalas.
pages.intro: Jungle and safari animals are a classic coloring theme that never fades: lions, elephants, giraffes and monkeys are instantly recognisable, and kids love the adventure of a safari. Here are five jungle and safari coloring books of 24 pages each: baby animals with their mothers for toddlers, a jungle explorer adventure, rainforest animals layer by layer, savanna wildlife and the great migration, and safari mandalas for adults. Each book is written out page by page, so you can paste one page at a time into ChatGPT, Gemini or any AI image tool, or copy all 24 and make the whole book.
keywords: jungle animal coloring book for kids
zoo animal coloring book for toddlers
tips: Keep rainforest and savanna in separate books; each then ranks for its own keywords and the pages barely overlap.
For toddlers, show baby animals with their mothers; for older kids, add explorers, jeeps and rope bridges to make it an adventure.
Elephants, lions and giraffes carry mandala patterns beautifully, which makes safari a good crossover into the adult market.

prompts.why: Tweens and homeschool parents want real animals in real habitats, and organising the book by rainforest layer turns it into a science resource as well as a coloring book.

pages.title: Cat Coloring Book Prompts: Kittens, Cozy Cats & Cat Mandalas
pages.metaDescription: Cat coloring book prompts for five 24-page books, page by page: playful kittens, cats around the world, 24 cat breeds, cozy cats and cat mandalas.
pages.intro: Cat lovers are one of the most loyal buyer groups on Amazon KDP and Etsy, and cat coloring books sell to kids, teens and adults alike. Here are five cat coloring books of 24 pages each, written out page by page: playful kittens for preschoolers, a cat travelling around the world, 24 cat breeds with names, cozy cat life for teens and adults, and a zen cat mandala collection. Copy one page at a time into ChatGPT, Gemini or any AI image tool, or copy all 24 and make the whole book.
tips: Cats in cozy settings (window seats, bookshops, houseplants, teacups) are a strong adult and teen sub-niche, often sold as gifts for cat owners.
A cat breeds book lets owners find their own cat; mention favourites like Maine Coon and Ragdoll in the listing.
For kids, give the cats a place to be, like a Paris café or a Venice gondola, so each page tells a tiny story.

pages.title: Space Coloring Book Prompts: Planets, Astronauts & Aliens
pages.metaDescription: Space coloring page prompts for five 24-page books, page by page: a toddler space trip, animal astronauts, named planets, alien worlds and retro cosmos.
pages.intro: Space coloring books mix wonder with learning, and they sell to curious kids, homeschoolers and adult colorists alike. Here are five space coloring books of 24 pages each: a first trip to space for toddlers, an animal astronaut crew, a planets and moons book with every object named, made-up alien worlds for tweens, and retro-futurist space scenes for adults. Each is written out page by page, so you can paste one page at a time into ChatGPT, Gemini or any AI image tool, or copy all 24 and make the whole book.
tips: A named planets-and-moons book ranks for educational keywords as well as coloring ones.
Animals in space helmets keep a young kid's space book playful instead of empty and dark.
Retro rockets and domed moon cities reach adult buyers who would skip plain planet pages.

pages.intro: Vehicle coloring books are a top seller for kids who love anything with wheels, wings or a horn. pages.intro: Princess coloring books are a perennial gift for young children, and fairy-tale castles keep their charm right into the adult coloring market. Here are five princess and castle coloring books of 24 pages each with original characters: a sweet little-princess day for toddlers, a knights-and-dragons adventure, princesses from many lands, a royal gown fashion book for teens, and ornate fairy-tale castles for adults. tips: Use only original princesses: anything that looks or sounds like a film character can get a KDP listing removed.

pages.intro: Mermaid coloring books combine magic and the ocean, and they sell as gifts from preschool to the tween years and to a strong adult audience. Here are five mermaid coloring books of 24 pages each with original characters: baby mermaids and sea friends for toddlers, a whole undersea kingdom, merfolk from Arctic ice to mangrove swamps, cozy everyday mermaid life for teens and adults, and ornate mermaid portraits. keywords: under the sea mermaid coloring pages
tips: Keep every mermaid original; avoid famous red-haired film mermaids and their sidekicks so the book is safe to sell.

Include merboys and mermaids of different looks, which broadens the gift audience.

pages.title: Robot Coloring Book Prompts for Kids & Tweens
pages.metaDescription: Robot coloring book prompts for five 24-page books, written page by page: toddler robots, town jobs, robot animals, giant mechs and steampunk machines.
pages.intro: Robot coloring books appeal to kids who love building and gadgets, and they make a good STEM-flavoured gift. Here are five robot coloring books of 24 pages each: friendly boxy robots for toddlers, a town where robots do every job, animals rebuilt as robots, giant mechs for teens, and brass steampunk automatons for adult colorists. Each book is written out page by page, so you can paste one page at a time into ChatGPT, Gemini or any AI image tool.
tips: Pitch robot books as STEM gifts in your listing; parents searching for science gifts are a wider audience than robot fans alone.
Toddler robots work best boxy, big-eyed and busy with everyday jobs like baking or gardening.
Avoid shape-shifting car robots and other famous designs; robot animals, mechs and steampunk bots are safe, original angles.

pages.intro: Mandala coloring books are one of the most reliable sellers on Amazon KDP, bought by adults who color to unwind and by teens who love symmetry. Here are five mandala coloring books of 24 pages each, with a different design on every page: first mandalas for kids, celestial boho mandalas for tweens, bold and easy mandalas for beginners, flower and botanical mandalas, and intricate geometric designs for experienced colorists. tips: Name the motifs you want (lotus petals, star polygons, paisley, lace) so each page gets a different design instead of twenty-four near-identical circles.

Sell a beginner and an intricate edition side by side; buyers who finish one often come back for the other.

pages.title: Stress Relief Coloring Book Prompts for Adults
pages.metaDescription: Stress relief coloring book prompts for five 24-page books, written page by page: calm shores, bedtime scenes, mandalas, a large-print garden and tweens.
pages.intro: These stress relief coloring book prompts are for adults who want a quiet way to slow down away from screens, for seniors who need bigger, simpler pictures, and for tweens getting through exam season. Each of the five books keeps to one setting: calm shores, a night-time wind-down, intricate pattern meditations, a large-print garden and everyday calm breaks for tweens. Every book is written out page by page, 24 pages each, so you can paste one page at a time into ChatGPT, Gemini or any AI image tool.
keywords: stress relief coloring book for adults
tips: Lean on slow, quiet subjects (still water, sleeping animals, rain, candlelight); calm scenes beat busy ones for this buyer.
Keep pages without words; many anxiety-relief buyers find affirmations distracting and prefer to let the picture do the work.
Give each book in the series one clear setting (shore, night, garden) so buyers can pick the one that relaxes them.

pages.intro: Cozy coloring books are a steady niche on Amazon KDP and Etsy: warm interiors, rainy windows, steaming mugs and little shops full of charm, for teens and adults who color to unwind and for easy gifts. Here are five cozy coloring books of 24 pages each: cottagecore countryside, a café and bakery book, an intricate bookshop and library edition, a snowy cabin winter, and animal-run shops for tweens. Each is written out page by page, so you can paste one page at a time into ChatGPT, Gemini or any AI image tool, or copy all 24 and make the whole book.
tips: Fill each room with small comforting objects (blankets, teapots, plants, string lights); the clutter is the charm.
Give each book one setting (cottage, café, bookshop, cabin) so the five read as a series rather than one mixed book.
Animal shopkeepers give a cozy book a character hook buyers remember, without leaning on any famous brand.

pages.title: Bold and Easy Coloring Book Prompts for Adults & Seniors
pages.metaDescription: Bold and easy coloring prompts for five 24-page books, written page by page: retro nostalgia, cute animals, sweet treats, little houses and beach days.
pages.intro: Bold and easy coloring books have big, simple shapes and large areas to fill, which makes them a top seller for adults who want quick relaxation, seniors, people with low vision and anyone using markers. Here are five bold and easy books of 24 pages each, one clear subject per page: retro nostalgia for seniors, cute animal friends, sweet treats and snacks, little houses and shops, and a day at the beach. Each book is written out page by page, so you can paste one page at a time into ChatGPT, Gemini or any AI image tool.
keywords: bold and easy coloring book prompts
bold and easy coloring book for adults
large print coloring book for seniors
coloring book for people with dementia
tips: Keep to one main subject per page; a teacup or a cactus with a few props reads better than a crowded scene.
Choose familiar, friendly objects; recognisable subjects are what make bold and easy books relaxing.
Market the books for alcohol markers and gel pens; big areas suit them and that is how buyers search.

pages.title: Flower & Botanical Coloring Book Prompts
pages.metaDescription: Flower and botanical coloring book prompts for five 24-page books, written page by page: vintage botanicals, bouquets, houseplants and wildflowers.
pages.intro: Flower and botanical coloring books are bought year-round by gardeners, nature lovers and adult colorists, and they are a favorite gift around Mother's Day and in spring. These five books each run 24 pages: an intricate vintage botanical edition, bouquets and flower-shop arrangements, succulents and houseplants, wildflowers with their pollinators for tweens, and big friendly flowers for preschoolers. Every book is written out page by page, so you can paste one page at a time into ChatGPT, Gemini or any AI image tool.
tips: Name real flowers (peony, foxglove, magnolia, iris); specific species look far better than a generic 'flower'.
For the botanical edition, ask for leaves, buds, seed pods and roots too; it gives the vintage herbarium look buyers want.
Time flower books for spring and Mother's Day, when gift searches for floral coloring books peak.

prompts.why: Adult colorists and gardeners pay a premium for realistic botanical detail, and the vintage herbarium angle stands out from generic flower books.

pages.title: Christmas Coloring Book Prompts for Kids & Adults
pages.metaDescription: Christmas coloring book prompts for five 24-page books, written page by page: toddlers, Santa's workshop, snow days, a cozy village and mandalas.
pages.intro: Christmas is the biggest seasonal sale of the year on Amazon KDP and Etsy, and demand starts in October. Here are five Christmas coloring books of 24 pages each, running from toddlers to adults: a first Christmas book for ages 3-6, a Santa's workshop adventure for ages 6-9, snow-day fun for tweens, a cozy village for adults and an intricate book of ornament and snowflake mandalas. Each one is written out page by page, so you can paste one page at a time into ChatGPT, Gemini or any AI image tool.
tips: Publish Christmas books by early October; the search peak runs from November to mid-December.
Mix classic symbols (stockings, wreaths, gingerbread) with full scenes so a 24-page book is not 24 lone ornaments.
Give the kids' and adult books one series name so buyers who find one find the rest.

pages.title: Halloween Coloring Book Prompts for Kids & Adults
pages.metaDescription: Halloween coloring page prompts for five 24-page books, written page by page: spooky-cute toddlers, a monster party, a haunted manor and mandalas.
pages.intro: Halloween coloring books sell from September through October to parents, teachers and adults who love the season. Here are five Halloween coloring books of 24 pages each: spooky-cute pumpkins and ghosts for ages 3-6, a monster party for ages 6-9, a room-by-room haunted manor for tweens, a witchy spooky-cozy cottage for adults and intricate moonlit mandalas. Each one is written out page by page, so you can paste one page at a time into ChatGPT, Gemini or any AI image tool, and the kids' books stay friendly, with no gore and no scary faces.
keywords: spooky cozy coloring book for adults
tips: Keep ghosts and monsters smiling for kids; spooky-cute sells, scary returns.
For adults, 'spooky-cozy' (witch cottages, candles, black cats, apothecary shelves) outsells horror on KDP.
Publish by early September so the books are indexed before the October rush.

pages.title: Easter & Spring Coloring Book Prompts
pages.metaDescription: Easter and spring coloring book prompts for five 24-page books, written page by page: toddler bunnies, an egg hunt, spring outdoors and folk-art eggs.
pages.intro: Easter and spring coloring books are basket fillers: parents, grandparents and teachers buy them in March and April, and adults pick up patterned egg and nature books for the season. These five prompts each make a 24-page book: bunnies and chicks for toddlers, an egg-hunt adventure for ages 6-9, spring outdoors for tweens, realistic baby animals for adults and an intricate book of folk-art decorated eggs. Every book is written out page by page, so you can paste one page at a time into ChatGPT, Gemini or any AI image tool.
tips: Market Easter books as basket stuffers; it is the phrase gift buyers search.
Mix Easter and general spring scenes (rain, gardens, baby animals) so the books sell beyond Easter week.
For adults, folk-art egg patterns give a seasonal twist on the mandala niche.

pages.intro: Autumn and Thanksgiving coloring books sell from September to late November: parents keep kids busy at the holiday table, teachers use them in class, and adults love the cozy fall mood. Here are five 24-page books: big leaves and pumpkins for toddlers, a Thanksgiving gratitude book for ages 6-9, fall outings for tweens, a cozy autumn-at-home book for adults and a realistic woodland-wildlife edition. Each one is written out page by page, so you can paste one page at a time into ChatGPT, Gemini or any AI image tool.
tips: Pair Thanksgiving with general autumn scenes so the books sell from September, not just one week in November.

pages.title: Alphabet ABC Coloring Book Prompts for Toddlers & Preschool
pages.metaDescription: Alphabet coloring page prompts for five ABC books of 24 to 26 pages, written page by page: animals, first words, phonics, jobs and a floral alphabet.
pages.intro: Alphabet coloring books sell all year to parents, preschool teachers and homeschoolers teaching letters. Here are five ABC coloring books written out page by page: an animal alphabet parade and a first-words picture dictionary for toddlers, a phonics book of letter sounds, vowels and letter teams, an A to Z of jobs and where people work, and a 24-page floral alphabet with numbers for adult colorists. The four A to Z books have 26 pages, one letter per page; copy one page at a time into ChatGPT, Gemini or any AI image tool, or copy them all and make the whole book.
tips: An alphabet is exactly 26 pages, so keep one letter per page and fold the extras into the same scenes (a vowel's long sound, a letter team, the workplace) instead of padding the book with repeats.
Pick words a child can say and picture; 'D drum' teaches the letter, 'D dulcimer' does not.
Sell the toddler books and the phonics book as a set; the parent buying one usually has a child heading into the next stage.

pages.title: Numbers & Counting Coloring Book Prompts for Kids
pages.metaDescription: Five 24-page counting coloring book prompts, written page by page: count to 8 three ways, numbers 1 to 20, make-ten math, ocean 1 to 40 and times tables.
pages.intro: Counting coloring books help children link a number to an amount, and parents, preschool teachers and homeschoolers use them at every stage. These five 24-page books cover counting to 8 three ways, numbers with a numeral page and a counting page, make-ten and teen-number math, counting to 40 under the sea, and times tables as equal groups. Each one is written out page by page with its caption, so you can paste one page at a time into ChatGPT, Gemini or any AI image tool.
tips: Write each page as a number and its objects ('7 crabs') so the count on the page matches the caption.
Use small, separate objects (pebbles, bubbles, pearls) for numbers above 20 so children can count them one by one.
For math pages, give one object per section (ladybugs for make-ten, cookies for doubles) so the page changes but the method stays the same.

pages.title: Shapes and Colors Coloring Book Prompts for Preschool
pages.metaDescription: Five 24-page shapes and colors coloring book prompts, written page by page: first shapes, first colors, 3D solids, 24 color names and tween geometry.
pages.intro: Shapes and colors are among the first things children learn, so these books suit parents, preschool teachers and homeschoolers from toddler to middle school. Here are five 24-page books: eight basic shapes in everyday things, eight first colors, 3D solids with shape hunt scenes, twenty-four color names, and a geometry book for tweens. Each one is written out page by page, so you can paste one page at a time into ChatGPT, Gemini or any AI image tool.
tips: Give each shape or color several real objects (three each fills 24 pages for eight shapes) so a child sees the same idea in new places.
In a colors book the caption is the instruction: the child colors the page in the named color, so pick objects that really are that color.
Shape hunt scenes work best in places children know (a kitchen, a playground), where there is plenty to spot.

Star: a starfish, a magic wand, a star lantern. Heart: a heart balloon, a heart cookie, a locket. Diamond: a kite, a gemstone, a diamond-patterned sock.

pages.title: Good Habits & Manners Coloring Book Prompts for Kids
pages.metaDescription: Five good habits and manners coloring books of 24 pages each, written page by page: toddler routines, animal manners, manners by place, health and tweens.
pages.intro: Good habits coloring books turn routines and manners into something children want to do, which is why parents, preschool teachers, counsellors and homeschoolers keep buying them. Here are five 24-page books with one habit per page and its caption: a toddler's day from morning to night, kind manners shown by animal friends, manners at the table, at school, in town and as a guest, health and safety habits, and responsibility for tweens. Each one is written out page by page, so you can paste one page at a time into ChatGPT, Gemini or any AI image tool.
keywords: daily routine coloring pages for toddlers
tips: Phrase every habit as an action ('carrying my plate to the sink') so each page is one clear picture with a caption that says what to do.
Group the 24 habits by time of day or by place; the book then reads in order and works as a routine chart.
Keep each book to its own age: toddlers want getting dressed and bath time, tweens want chores, money and screen habits.

pages.title: Feelings & Emotions Coloring Book Prompts for Kids
pages.metaDescription: Five 24-page feelings coloring book prompts, written page by page: animal feelings, feeling words, a calm-down toolbox, tween moments and emotion weather.
pages.intro: Feelings coloring books give children words for what they feel, and parents, preschool teachers, school counsellors and homeschoolers use them for social-emotional learning. These five 24-page books cover eight feelings shown by baby animals, 24 feeling words, a calm-down toolbox of 24 strategies, 24 real-life moments for tweens, and 24 emotions pictured as weather and nature for teens and adults. Each one is written out page by page, so you can paste one page at a time into ChatGPT, Gemini or any AI image tool.
keywords: calm down coloring book for kids
tips: Pair a feeling with a moment ('sad: a balloon floating away'); a situation teaches more than a face.
Use animal characters for little ones, so a child can talk about a feeling without it being about them.
Counsellors often buy a feelings book and a calm-down book together; list them as a pair.

prompts.name: Eight feelings with animal friends
prompts.brief: A first feelings book: eight feelings, each shown by baby animals in three moments, one per page with the feeling as its caption. Happy: puppy with a new ball, piglet in mud, lamb on a swing. Sad: lost balloon, washed-away sandcastle, broken toy train. Angry: tower knocked over, skipped in line, tangled kite. Scared: thunder, a dark bedroom, owlet's first flight. Surprised: a present, first snow, a surprise party. Proud: tying a shoelace, winning a race, a drawing. Shy: new friends, first school day, hiding behind mom. Calm: hammock, cloud watching, slow breathing.
prompts.why: Preschool teachers and parents use animal feelings books to start conversations, and three moments per feeling help a child see that a feeling can come from many things.
settings: One item per page, with its caption

pages.title: Greek Mythology Coloring Book Prompts
pages.metaDescription: Greek mythology coloring book prompts for five 24-page books, written page by page: nature myths, a creature bestiary, hero quests, gods and the Odyssey.
pages.intro: Greek mythology coloring books are for kids who devour myth stories, homeschoolers teaching ancient history, and teens and adults who love epic heroes and monsters, and because the myths are public domain they are a safe niche for KDP sellers. Here are five books of 24 pages each: nature myths that explain the seasons and the stars for ages 6 to 9, a bestiary of legendary creatures, the heroes' quests in order, a gallery of gods, Titans and Muses for adults, and the Trojan War and the Odyssey in story order. Each book is written out page by page, so you can paste one page at a time into ChatGPT, Gemini or any AI image tool.
keywords: greek mythology coloring book for adults
greek mythology coloring book for kids
tips: Name the exact myth moment (Perseus with the mirrored shield, Odysseus tied to the mast) rather than just the hero; scenes sell better than portraits.
Keep the monsters dramatic without gore: the Minotaur in the labyrinth works, the fight's aftermath does not.
Homeschoolers pair these with ancient history units, so a book that tells the Trojan War or Hercules' labors in order sells well to them.

prompts.why: Parents and teachers want a way into the classic myths for ages 6 to 9, and myths that explain seasons, spiders and stars answer questions kids already ask.

prompts.name: Quests of the Greek heroes
prompts.brief: The great Greek hero quests in 24 scenes, one per page, in story order. Hercules: the Nemean lion, the hydra, the golden hind, the Augean stables, the Stymphalian birds, holding up the sky for Atlas, Cerberus. Perseus: winged sandals, the Graeae's eye, the mirrored shield and Medusa, rescuing Andromeda. Theseus: his father's sword, Ariadne's thread, the Minotaur. prompts.why: Middle-grade myth fans and homeschoolers want the hero stories told in order, and seven of Hercules' labors plus seven other heroes' quests make a book that teaches the stories as well as being colored.

pages.title: Bible Story Coloring Book Prompts for Kids & Adults
pages.metaDescription: Bible story coloring book prompts written page by page: five 24-page books of Bible animals, Old Testament stories, Jesus' life, parables and scripture.
pages.intro: Bible story coloring books are a steady seller for Christian parents, Sunday school teachers, church groups and homeschoolers, with peaks at Easter and Christmas. Here are five Bible story coloring books of 24 pages each: animals of the Bible for toddlers, Old Testament stories in order, the life of Jesus from the angel's visit to Pentecost, twenty-four parables Jesus told, and detailed scripture-inspired scenes for adult colorists, all drawn from public-domain stories. Each book is written out page by page, so you can paste one page at a time into ChatGPT, Gemini or any AI image tool, or copy all 24 and make the whole book.
tips: Name the exact moment (Zacchaeus up the sycamore tree, the walls of Jericho falling) so each page is recognisable.
For children's books choose the moment before the danger: David with his sling facing Goliath, Daniel among the lions.
Sunday school teachers buy books that follow the Bible's order, so one Old Testament book and one life-of-Jesus book can run a whole year.

pages.title: Bedtime Story Coloring Book Prompts for Calm Evenings
pages.metaDescription: Five 24-page bedtime story coloring books, written page by page: a badger's lost blanket, a city walk, a sleeper train, a lighthouse cat, a dream sheep.
pages.intro: A bedtime story coloring book gives the last half hour of the day a shape: color a page, read its line or two, turn to the next. Here are five bedtime stories of 24 pages each for ages 3 to 13, from a badger cub hunting for his blanket and a girl's goodnight walk around the block to a sleeper train, a lighthouse cat and a dream ride with the hundredth sheep. Each book is written out page by page, with the picture and the words for every page, so you can paste one page at a time into ChatGPT, Gemini or any AI image tool.
tips: Twenty-four pages is a gentle bedtime read; color three or four pages a night and the book lasts a week.
Give the story a clock (dusk, lamps on, moonrise, bed) so each run of pages sits later in the evening.
Selling several on KDP? Keep each book's hero and setting distinct, like these five, so the titles don't compete.

prompts.name: Bramble the badger cub's lost blanket
prompts.brief: A 24-page bedtime story. Bramble, a badger cub with a white stripe and pajamas too big for him, cannot find his patchwork blanket at bedtime. He searches the twilight wood: under the ferns, at the rabbits' burrow, the frog pond, the owl's oak, the hedgehogs' leaf pile, the squirrels' nest, the fireflies' meadow and the old stone wall where the moths sleep. Each friend points him onward. In a hollow log he finds the blanket, now a nest for five baby mice. He shares it, they all fall asleep, and Mama Badger finds them under the moon.
prompts.why: Parents of toddlers get a full 24-page goodnight story that visits one sleepy animal home after another and ends with the hero asleep.

pageTexts: The sun was going down over the wood, and Bramble the badger cub gave a great big yawn.
It was bedtime, but his patchwork blanket was not on his bed. "Where is my blanket?" said Bramble.
He looked under the ferns. No blanket there, just a ladybird fast asleep.
He asked Mother Rabbit. "We haven't seen it," she said. "Ask the frogs at the pond."
So Bramble set off down the path, holding up his too-long pajamas.
The frogs were singing their goodnight song. "Ribbit, goodnight! Ribbit, sleep tight!"
"No blanket here," said Big Frog. "Ask the owl in the old oak."
Owl was just waking up. "I go to work at night," said Owl, "but I have not seen a blanket. Try the hedgehogs."
The hedgehogs were curling up in their leaves. "No blanket in here," they yawned.
High in the tree, the squirrels called down, "Follow the fireflies! They see everything."
In the meadow, the fireflies lit up one by one, like tiny lamps.
They led Bramble over the little bridge, blink, blink, blink.
At the old stone wall, a soft moth landed on his nose. "I know where it is," she whispered.
"Look in the hollow log," said the moth. Bramble tiptoed closer.
There it was! A corner of his patchwork blanket, poking out of the log.
Bramble peeked inside. Five baby mice were snuggled up on his blanket, warm and cozy.
"I'm sorry," said Mother Mouse. "My babies were so cold tonight."
Bramble sat down and thought. It was his blanket. But the mice were so small.
"There is room for everyone," said Bramble, and he crawled inside.
He pulled the blanket over himself and all five baby mice. It was the coziest bed in the wood.
Back home, Mama Badger took her lantern and went looking for Bramble.
She found him in the hollow log, fast asleep with his new friends. She smiled.
Mama Badger curled up beside the log, and the big moon kept watch over them all.
Goodnight, Bramble. Goodnight, little mice. Goodnight, wood.

pageTexts: After dinner, Dad zipped Noor's coat right over her star pajamas. "Time for our goodnight walk," he said.
Down the front steps they went, hand in hand, out into the evening street.
Mr. Hamid the baker was pulling down his shutter. "Goodnight, Noor! Fresh bread tomorrow!"
The florist was carrying her flowers inside. Noor held the door for the sunflowers.
At the corner shop, the grocer stacked his crates up high. One apple sat on top like a hat.
The bus came to its very last stop. The driver stretched her arms. Her day was done.
On the bridge, the pigeons tucked their heads under their wings. Goodnight, pigeons.
At the park, the swings were empty. The park keeper locked the gate. Goodnight, park.
Three dogs trotted home for supper. The smallest one sniffed Noor's boots to say goodnight.
A sleepy cat watched from her window. Noor waved, and the cat blinked slowly back.
A nurse walked past on her way to work. "Some people work while we sleep," said Dad.
Click, click, click! The streetlights came on, one after another, all down the street.
From up on Dad's shoulders, Noor saw the Moon rise between the buildings.
Then it was home again, up the stairs. Noor counted every step.
Splish, splash! Noor had a warm bubble bath with her little boat.
Dad dried her curly hair with the fluffiest towel. It tickled!
Brush, brush, brush. Top teeth, bottom teeth, all clean.
On went the star pajamas again, and Ellie the elephant waited on the bed.
Noor chose one story from the shelf. Just one, because it was late.
Dad read the story, and Noor's eyes grew heavy.
Noor knelt at the window. "Goodnight, Moon. Goodnight, street."
Down below, the shops were dark and the street was quiet.
Dad turned on the little moon light. "Goodnight, Noor," he whispered.
And Noor was fast asleep, with Ellie in her arms and the Moon in her window.

pageTexts: The big station clock said seven o'clock. Theo held his mom's hand and stared at the long night train.
The conductor held up her brass lantern. "Tickets, please! And who is this?" "This is Parsnip," said Theo.
Their cabin was tiny, with two bunks, a sink and a window. Theo bounced on the bed. It was perfect.
He unpacked his toothbrush, his flashlight and his pajamas, and gave Parsnip the top pillow.
With a jolt and a whistle, the train began to move. Theo waved until the station was gone.
Back gardens rushed by: washing lines, sheds and a boy on a fence who waved back.
Then came the fields, gold and wide, and the sun sank down behind the hills.
In the dining car, they ate warm soup with crusty rolls while the world went by.
At a crossing, a farmer on a tractor waited for them. Ding, ding, ding went the bell.
A little town slid past, sleepy and still, with only a few lights left on.
The conductor let Theo look at her lantern. "It has lit the way on this train for forty years," she said.
Brushing your teeth on a train is tricky. The whole cabin swayed, and Theo giggled.
Up the ladder he climbed to the top bunk, with Parsnip under his arm.
Whoosh! Into a tunnel. Theo counted the lights. Ten, eleven, twelve...
Out by a lake, two deer lifted their heads as the train went by in the moonlight.
The train rumbled over a tall stone bridge, high above a river far below.
Mom read a chapter from his book. Theo listened, and his eyes grew heavy.
An owl on a fence post watched the train go by. Hoo, hoo, goodnight.
Clickety-clack, clickety-clack. The train rocked Theo gently to sleep.
At midnight, the conductor walked softly down the corridor with her lantern. All was well.
All night long, the train climbed up and up into the mountains.
In the morning, Theo pulled up the blind. Snow! Mountains everywhere, pink in the sunrise.
The train slowed and stopped at a little snowy station.
And there was Grandma, with a big hug and a thermos of hot cocoa. "You made it!"

prompts.name: Marigold the lighthouse cat
prompts.brief: A 24-page bedtime story. Marigold, an orange cat with one white paw, lives in a lighthouse on a rocky island with the keeper, Mr. Penrose. Every evening she climbs the 99 spiral steps to watch him light the lamp, then follows the beam across the sea. Tonight it sweeps over fishing boats heading in, seals on the rocks, the late ferry, puffins in their burrows, a sailboat with a torn sail that the beam guides into the harbor, a whale and leaping dolphins, and the village going dark window by window. When every boat is tied up, Marigold curls up on the keeper's armchair and sleeps.

pageTexts: On a rocky island far out at sea lived Marigold, an orange cat with one white paw, and Mr. Penrose, the lighthouse keeper.
Every evening began the same way: fish for Marigold and a pot of tea for Mr. Penrose.
Then up they went, ninety-nine spiral steps. Marigold always got to the top first.
Mr. Penrose polished the great glass lens until it shone. Marigold watched a hundred little cats look back at her.
He struck a long match, and the lamp burst into light. The night's work had begun.
Marigold sat on the railing and followed the beam as it swept round and round across the sea.
The beam found the fishing boats coming home, with full nets and hungry gulls behind them.
It passed over the seals on the rocks. A little pup blinked up at the light.
The late ferry crossed the bay, its windows glowing like a string of beads.
On the cliff, the puffins were going to bed in their burrows, one with a last fishy snack.
Then the wind picked up and the waves grew tall. Mr. Penrose lifted his binoculars. "Look, Marigold. Someone's out there."
A little sailboat was tossing on the waves, its sail torn, its sailor all alone.
Round came the beam, and it shone a bright path straight across the water. "Follow the light!" Marigold seemed to say.
The sailboat followed the beam all the way into the harbor, safe and sound.
Later, when the sea was calm again, a whale rose up in the moonlight and blew a great spout.
Two dolphins leaped right through the beam, as if they were playing in it.
Across the bay, the village went to sleep, one window at a time.
The last fisherman tied up his boat and walked home with his lantern. Every boat was in.
Mr. Penrose wrote it all in the logbook. Marigold helped by lying on the page.
"Good work tonight, Marigold," he said, and gave her a sardine.
Then Marigold padded back down the ninety-nine steps, much more slowly this time.
Her favorite chair was waiting by the warm stove.
She curled up, and Mr. Penrose tucked the blanket around her. "Goodnight, little keeper."
And the light kept turning all night long, over a calm sea where every boat was safely home.

prompts.name: Ivy and the hundredth sheep
prompts.brief: A 24-page bedtime story. Ivy, ten, with a long braid and round glasses, can't fall asleep and starts counting sheep. The hundredth one, a sheep named Woolsey in a nightcap, stops, steps into her room and offers her a ride on a cloud. They float over the sleeping town to the dream islands: a library with pillow shelves, a night bakery making moon-shaped rolls, a river of warm milk with paper boats, an observatory where owls polish the stars, a garden of glowing night flowers and a hammock field. As the sky turns grey, Woolsey tucks Ivy back into bed, and she is asleep before he leaves.
prompts.why: Parents of older kids who resist bedtime get a 24-page dream adventure with real places to color and a story that ends back in bed.

Ivy stretched out in a hammock and yawning, her braid hanging over the side, Woolsey standing up and pointing toward the sky.
Ivy and Woolsey riding the cloud home as the sky turns pale grey at the edges, the sleeping town and the river coming into view below.
Woolsey tucking Ivy back into her bed under her quilt, the cloud waiting outside the open window and her slippers lined up on the rug.
Ivy fast asleep and smiling, her glasses folded on the nightstand, Woolsey slipping out of the window on his cloud, one tuft of wool left on her pillow.
pageTexts: It was way past bedtime, and Ivy was wide awake. The clock ticked. The Moon stared in. Sleep would not come.
"Fine," Ivy sighed. "I'll count sheep." One sheep jumped the fence. Then two. Then three.
Ninety-seven, ninety-eight, ninety-nine... but sheep number one hundred did not jump. He stopped right on top of the fence and looked at her.
Then he stepped down onto her bedroom rug. "Good evening," said the sheep. "I'm Woolsey. You seem to be having trouble sleeping."
Woolsey opened the window. A cloud was waiting there, soft as a pillow. "Shall we go for a ride?"
Ivy pulled on her dressing gown and slippers and climbed out onto the cloud. It was like stepping into whipped cream.
They floated over the rooftops of her town. Everyone she knew was asleep down there.
They passed the clock tower just as it struck midnight, and the river shone silver below.
Then, ahead in the stars, Ivy saw them: the dream islands, floating in the sky and joined by little rope bridges.
The first island was a library where the shelves were made of pillows, so the books could rest too.
Ivy found a cozy nook and read. Around her, books flapped their pages and flew from shelf to shelf.
On the next island was a bakery that only opened at night. The mole baker made rolls shaped like the Moon.
Ivy and Woolsey shared a warm roll. It tasted like honey and sleepy Sunday mornings.
Beyond the bakery flowed a river of warm milk, carrying hundreds of tiny paper boats.
"Every boat is someone's wish for tomorrow," said Woolsey. Ivy folded one of her own and set it sailing.
On the highest island stood an observatory, where owls worked all night polishing the stars.
An owl handed Ivy a star and a cloth. She rubbed until it glowed, and the owl hung it back in the sky.
Through the great telescope, Ivy could see every crater on the Moon, close enough to touch.
In the night garden, flowers glowed softly, and moths drifted from bloom to bloom.
The last island was a field of hammocks. Woolsey flopped into one and pulled his nightcap over his eyes.
Ivy climbed into a hammock and gave an enormous yawn. "Time to go home," said Woolsey gently.
They floated back over the town as the sky turned grey at the edges. Morning was on its way.
Woolsey tucked Ivy into her own bed and smoothed the quilt. "Sleep well, Ivy."
She was asleep before he reached the window. In the morning, there was a tuft of wool on her pillow.

pages.title: First Day of School Story Coloring Book Prompts
pages.theme: First Day of School Story Coloring Book
pages.metaDescription: First day of school story coloring book prompts: five 24-page stories written page by page, from preschool to a new school and middle school.
pages.intro: A first day of school story coloring book lets a child rehearse the day before it happens: the walk in, the cubby, the teacher, the first friend, pickup. Here are five 24-page story books that each follow one hero through one first day, from a hedgehog starting preschool to an eleven-year-old opening a locker on day one of middle school. Every book is written out page by page, with the picture and the line of story for each page, so you can paste one page at a time into ChatGPT, Gemini or any AI image tool, or copy all 24 and make the whole book.
keywords: first day of school story coloring book
back to school story coloring book
tips: Follow the real day in order (morning, arrival, lessons, lunch, recess, pickup); 24 pages gives every part of the day its own page or two.
Match the school to the child: preschool, kindergarten, a new town or middle school each have different moments to show.
List back-to-school titles in July so they rank before the August rush.

pageTexts: It was a big day. Hazel the hedgehog was starting preschool!
Hazel ate her berries and toast. Her tummy felt a little wobbly.
She packed her lunchbox, her spare socks and Beetle, her very best toy.
Mom tied a bright red bow on her quills. "Ready?" asked Mom.
They walked past the pond. The ducks said quack, quack, good morning.
There was Acorn Hill Preschool, under the great big oak tree.
Hazel hugged Mom tight. "I will come back at pickup," Mom said.
"Welcome, Hazel," said Mrs. Badger. "We are so glad you came."
Hazel found her very own cubby with an acorn on it. In went her backpack.
At circle time everyone sang a clapping song.
Hazel did not feel like singing yet. She held Beetle close.
Then it was painting time. Hazel painted a big yellow sun.
The mole next to her painted a worm. "I'm Dot," she said. "I like your sun."
Hazel and Dot built a tall, tall tower. Crash! They both giggled.
At snack time Dot spilled her berries. Hazel shared hers.
They washed their paws together. Bubbles, bubbles everywhere!
Mrs. Badger read a story about a little boat that was brave.
Then it was time to rest. Hazel and Dot had mats side by side.
Outside, Hazel filled buckets and Dot dug a long tunnel.
Whee! Hazel went down the slide, and Dot came right after.
Everyone helped tidy up. Hazel put the blocks away.
There was Mom at the gate! Hazel ran to show her the sun painting.
"I made a friend," said Hazel. "Her name is Dot."
That night Hazel smiled in bed. Tomorrow she would sit with Dot again.

Mateo walking back into the classroom, Ms. Okafor smiling at him and a classmate with a gap-toothed grin waving from a table.
Mateo carrying a lunch tray with a carton of milk, an apple and a sandwich through a busy cafeteria with long tables.
Mateo at the lunch table opening his lunchbox to find a folded napkin with a heart drawn on it, the gap-toothed classmate sitting beside him.
Recess: Mateo running across the playground playing tag, his sneakers flashing, classmates scattering and laughing around him.
Mateo and his new friend swinging side by side on the playground swings, feet kicked high, a climbing frame behind them.
Mateo in a paint smock at an art table painting a big spiky dinosaur, paint cups, brushes and a jar of water beside his paper.
Mateo and his classmates putting chairs up on the tables at the end of the day, Ms. Okafor waving goodbye by the door.

pageTexts: Mateo woke up early. Today was his first day of kindergarten!
He put on his new sneakers. Stomp, stomp! They lit up with every step.
Abuela made pancakes, his favorite. "For a big kindergarten boy," she said.
Mateo zipped up his dinosaur backpack. It was almost bigger than him.
He held Abuela's hand all the way down the street.
At the corner the crossing guard held up her sign. Mateo gave her a high five.
All the kindergartners lined up by the big red door.
"Good morning, Mateo," said his teacher. "I'm Ms. Okafor."
Mateo hung his backpack on his very own hook.
Everyone sat on the big rug. Mateo put his hand up to say hello.
At show-and-tell Mateo held up Stego. "He has plates on his back," he said.
The class went to the library. Mateo found a book full of dinosaurs.
Later Mateo went to the bathroom and washed his hands all by himself.
But on the way back, every door looked the same. Where was his class?
A big girl stopped. "Are you lost? Your room is right down there."
Mateo was back! A boy named Ben waved at him from his table.
At lunch the cafeteria was big and loud. Mateo held his tray tight.
Abuela had put a heart in his lunchbox. Ben sat right next to him.
At recess they played tag. Mateo's sneakers flashed as he ran.
Mateo and Ben swung as high as the sky.
In art Mateo painted the biggest dinosaur he could.
At the end of the day everyone helped put the chairs up. "See you tomorrow!"
There was Abuela at the gate! Mateo ran to her as fast as he could.
All the way home Mateo told Abuela everything. "Can I go back tomorrow?"

pageTexts: Priya's new bedroom was full of boxes. Out the window, Willow Creek looked very quiet after the city.
"First day at a new school," said Mom, brushing her ponytail. Priya's stomach did a flip.
At the bus stop there was no subway, just a long road and a field of corn. Then the yellow bus came.
Priya sat by herself and watched the barns and cows go by. Everyone else seemed to know each other.
The bus stopped at Willow Creek Elementary. A huge willow tree stood by the front door.
In the office a kind woman gave Priya a paper with her room number on it.
Priya opened the first door she found. It was full of kindergartners! Wrong room.
The next door was right. "You must be Priya," said Mr. Hale. "Welcome to third grade."
"This is Rosa," said Mr. Hale. "She will be your class buddy today." Rosa waved hard.
Rosa showed Priya her desk. "I put a star on it for you," she said.
"Want to feed Mr. Slow?" asked Rosa. Priya had never fed a snail before.
In science they used magnets. Priya's paper clips made the longest chain in the class.
In math Mr. Hale asked Priya to draw a pattern on the board. She got it right.
Lunch was outside under the big oak tree. Rosa traded Priya a cookie for a grape.
"What are your patches?" asked Rosa. Priya told her all about the city.
At recess the class played soccer. Priya scored a goal!
"You're really fast," said Rosa, puffing. Priya grinned.
After lunch the class worked in the school garden. Priya watered the tomatoes.
Priya pulled up a carrot as long as her arm. Everyone laughed.
After school there was comic club in the library. "Come with me," said Rosa.
Priya drew a comic about a new girl and a snail. Rosa said it was the best one.
When the bell rang, Priya and Rosa hugged by the buses. "See you tomorrow!"
On the bus home Priya drew a map of her new school, so she would never get lost again.
"This is my classroom, and this is where Rosa and I eat lunch," Priya said. Willow Creek felt like home.

pageTexts: Gloop was starting first grade at Mossy Bog Monster School. Mom packed his favourite lunch: mud pies.
Gloop wiggled his one wobbly tooth. What if the other monsters were bigger and scarier than him?
The school bus was a giant caterpillar. It crawled up to the stop on a hundred wiggly legs.
Gloop sat between a monster with one huge eye and a monster with curly tentacles. Bump, bump, bump!
Mossy Bog Monster School was a swamp full of hollow tree stumps, each one a classroom.
Gloop's classroom was inside the biggest stump of all. The desks were toadstools!
"Good morning, little monsters," boomed Professor Grizzle. "I am your teacher."
First was roaring class. Everyone roared ROAR! Gloop opened his mouth and went... squeak.
Gloop felt silly. Then a fluffy monster tapped his shoulder. "I'm Fern. I like your squeak."
Next was puddle-jumping. Gloop and Fern made the biggest splash in the whole bog.
In cave painting Gloop pressed his hand on the wall. Now everyone would know he was there.
In counting class they counted fireflies in a jar. Gloop counted twelve. Fern counted thirteen.
At lunch Gloop and Fern shared mud pies. Gloopy, gloppy, delicious!
Crunch! Gloop's wobbly tooth popped right out into his mud pie. "You lost a tooth!" cried Fern.
At recess they went down the slime slide. Squelch! Whoosh!
Then they swung on the vines, higher and higher over the moss.
Professor Grizzle counted to ten for hide-and-seek. All the little monsters ran.
Gloop was small, so he hid under a bucket. Nobody could find him at all.
"Gloop wins!" called Professor Grizzle. Being small was good for something after all.
In music class Gloop played the bone xylophone. Plink, plonk, plink!
The music made Gloop feel brave. He took a deep breath and ROARED. Professor Grizzle gave him a gold star.
At the end of the day the caterpillar bus was waiting. Gloop held Fern's hand.
Gloop and Fern rode home side by side, waving to the frogs in the reeds.
"I lost a tooth, I found a roar and I made a friend," said Gloop. "Monster school is the best."

pageTexts: The night before sixth grade, Jonah practiced his locker combination over and over. Right, left, right. It never opened the same way twice.
He lay awake thinking about seven classes, a building twice the size of his old school and a locker that might never open.
In the morning Dad handed him his lunch. "Middle school," Dad said. "You've got this."
Jonah rode his bike to Ridgeview Middle School, wind in his messy hair and butterflies in his stomach.
The bike rack was jammed. Everybody looked older, taller and like they knew exactly where to go.
In the gym a teacher handed him his schedule. Seven classes, seven rooms, and only four minutes between them.
Then came locker 214. Jonah spun the dial three times. Nothing. He tried again. Still nothing.
An eighth grader stopped. "Lift the handle while you turn the last number," he said. Click! It opened.
Jonah found Room 108 and walked in. A whole room of eighth graders stared at him. Wrong lab.
The right lab was next door. His lab partner was a girl named Ana. "I got lost too," she whispered.
Their first experiment was a fizzing volcano. It foamed all over the bench, and they both cracked up.
In math the teacher said, "Pop quiz, just to see what you know." Jonah took a deep breath and did his best.
The hallways were a river of people. Jonah held his planner like a map and made it to every class on time.
Then came lunch. The cafeteria was so loud Jonah could barely think, and every seat seemed taken.
"Jonah! Over here!" It was Ana. Her friends slid over to make room.
With ten minutes of lunch left, Jonah found the library. It was quiet and calm, his new favorite spot.
In band Jonah picked the clarinet. His first note came out as a squeak, and the whole row laughed with him.
In gym they ran laps. By the last one Jonah was tired, but he was still smiling.
In social studies they spun the globe and talked about places to explore this year.
Finally the last bell rang, and the whole school poured into the hallways at once.
Jonah walked up to his locker, lifted the handle and turned the dial. It opened on the very first try.
At the bike rack Ana waved. "See you in science, partner!"
At dinner Jonah told his family everything: the wrong lab, the volcano, the squeaky clarinet and his new friend.
That night he wrote in his planner: Day one, done. He couldn't wait for day two.

pages.intro: A new baby sibling story coloring book gives an older child something of their own while the house fills with baby things. Here are five 24-page stories that each follow one family from the waiting to the first weeks or months together: a bunny who paints the nursery, a four-year-old big brother, a big sister of twins, an otter who teaches his little sister to swim and a nine-year-old whose family adopts a baby girl. Each book is written out page by page, with the picture and the line of story for every page, so you can paste one page at a time into ChatGPT, Gemini or any AI image tool.

tips: Twenty-four pages fits the whole arc: waiting, the birth or arrival, coming home, and the first weeks of life together.
Write a separate version per family shape (big sister, big brother, twins, adoption) so buyers find the exact match.
Put the older child's own job, like singing, fetching diapers or reading, into the story's last pages.

pageTexts: One spring morning, Mama and Papa had big news. "A baby is coming," said Mama, "and you are going to be a big sister."
Juniper pressed her floppy ear to Mama's tummy. She heard a tiny swish, swish.
The carrots in the garden grew and grew, and so did Mama's tummy.
At bedtime Juniper wondered about the baby. Would it hop? Would it play with her?
Papa painted the little room for the baby. Juniper helped paint orange carrots all along the wall.
Papa built a wooden cradle, and Juniper held the box of pegs.
In her toy box Juniper found her old baby rattle. "The baby can have this," she said.
Juniper sorted tiny socks into pairs. They were so small they fit on her paw!
Every evening Juniper read a story to the baby in Mama's tummy.
One night Mama said, "It is time!" Grandma Rabbit came hopping over to stay with Juniper.
Juniper and Grandma baked carrot muffins and waited for the telephone to ring.
In the morning Papa called. "Come and meet your baby brother!" Juniper picked daisies on the way.
There in Mama's arms was a tiny bunny with a pink nose. "This is Sprout," said Mama.
Juniper shook her old rattle very gently. Sprout opened one sleepy eye.
Sprout came home to the burrow. Juniper held the door open wide.
Sprout cried. He cried at breakfast, he cried at lunch, and he cried at bedtime too.
When Sprout slept, everyone whispered. Juniper could not bounce her ball at all.
Mama was busy with Sprout all day long. Juniper felt left out and a little sad.
Papa sat with her in the garden. "Sprout is lucky to have a big sister like you," he said.
One evening Sprout would not stop crying. Mama rocked and Papa hummed, but nothing worked.
Juniper leaned over the cradle and sang her carrot song: "Crunch, crunch, carrots in a row, sleepy little bunny, down you go."
Sprout stopped crying. He looked up at Juniper and gave a tiny yawn.
From then on, Juniper sang the carrot song to Sprout every single night.
"I am Sprout's big sister," said Juniper, "and I know just the song he likes."

Kai zoomed around the living room in his cape. "Big Brother Kai to the rescue!" he shouted.

Kai helped pack the hospital bag: a tiny hat, tiny socks and the whale.

Kai tucked the stuffed whale next to Lani. "He's yours now," he whispered.

Dad helped Kai hold Lani on the couch. She was warm and very small.

pageTexts: At dinner Mom held up two little pictures. "Two babies?" gasped Rosa. "Twins!" said Dad.
Rosa counted on her fingers: one big sister and two baby brothers. Her family was growing fast.
Suddenly everything came in twos. Dad built two cribs while Rosa read out the instructions.
Two car seats filled the back of the car. Rosa squeezed into the middle and wondered where her knees would go.
Rosa folded two of every tiny hat, two of every sock and two of every sleepsuit.
Mom's tummy grew so big that Rosa measured it every Sunday with a tape measure.
Leo and Max were born on a rainy Tuesday. Rosa pressed her nose against the nursery window.
The twins looked exactly alike: the same round cheeks, the same tiny noses, the same wisps of hair.
Then Rosa spotted it: a tiny freckle on Max's left ear. "Now I can always tell you apart!"
The twins came home, and Rosa became the house twin expert.
Bath time was double bath time. Rosa held two towels, one for each brother.
At three in the morning the twins cried together. Dad walked up and down with one baby on each shoulder.
Mom fed both babies at once, so Rosa brought her a glass of water without spilling a drop.
The double stroller was as wide as the sidewalk. Neighbors had to step onto the grass to let them pass.
Grandpa mixed the twins up every visit. "That's Max," giggled Rosa, pointing at the freckle.
Two babies meant a mountain of diapers. Rosa held her nose and passed the wipes.
When Rosa made her silliest face, Leo smiled. A second later, Max smiled too.
At tummy time Max rolled over first. Leo rolled right into Rosa's lap.
At show-and-tell Rosa told her whole class everything she knew about twins.
Some days Rosa missed having Mom to herself. So while the twins napped, they baked cookies, just the two of them.
Then came first foods. Leo threw peas, Max blew carrot bubbles, and the wall got the most of all.
Soon the twins could crawl, always in opposite directions. Rosa ran after them both.
For the twins' first birthday, Rosa hung streamers and helped bake two small cakes.
Rosa helped Leo and Max blow out one candle each. "Happy birthday, double trouble," she said with her gap-toothed grin.

pageTexts: Tumble woke up in the den and rubbed his eyes. A tiny new pup was curled up on Mama's tummy.
"This is your sister, Ripple," said Mama. Ripple sneezed right on Tumble's whiskers.
Ripple could not swim yet. She rode on Mama's tummy while Mama floated down the river.
When Ripple was bigger, she touched the water. "Too cold! Too wet!" she squeaked.
Tumble showed her how to float. "Lie back and look at the sky," he said.
Where the river ran fast, Tumble held Ripple's paw so the water could not pull them apart.
Next Tumble taught her to dive. Down they went, with bubbles trailing behind.
Under a stone Tumble found a crayfish. Ripple looked too, and found a pebble.
She tried again and again. At last Ripple caught a crayfish all by herself!
Then Tumble cracked a mussel on a flat stone, right on his tummy. Tap, tap, crack!
Ripple tried. The stone slipped and the mussel bonked her on the nose.
Ripple tried once more. Tap, tap, crack! She opened her very first mussel.
Then came the best lesson of all: sliding! Tumble whooshed down the muddy bank. Splash!
Ripple stood at the top of the slide. It looked very, very high.
"We'll go together," said Tumble. Whee! They slid down side by side.
After all that mud, Tumble showed Ripple how to comb her fur until it was fluffy.
A heron landed in the shallows. "Shh, let's hide," whispered Tumble, and they ducked into the reeds.
The heron flapped away over the trees. Ripple let out a big breath.
At nap time all the otters floated together, holding paws so no one drifted off.
Every day Ripple swam a little farther on her own.
One day Ripple looked across the river. "I want to swim to the far bank by myself," she said.
She paddled and kicked, all the way across, while Tumble and Mama cheered.
Ripple climbed onto the far bank. "I did it!" she called.
"Race you home!" called Tumble. Brother and sister splashed back to the den, side by side.

pageTexts: On a Saturday morning, Mom and Dad sat Eli down at the kitchen table. "We're going to adopt a baby," Mom said. Eli nearly dropped his camera.
First came the paperwork, a stack of forms as thick as a dictionary. Eli took a photo of it, just for proof.
Ms. Alvarez, the social worker, came to visit. She asked what kind of big brother Eli would be. "The kind who takes lots of pictures," he said.
That spring they turned the spare room into a nursery. Eli painted the walls with a roller taller than he was.
Dad put the crib together, and Eli hung a mobile of paper birds he had folded himself.
Then they waited. Months went by on the kitchen calendar, and every time the phone buzzed, everyone jumped.
Summer turned into fall. Some days Eli wondered if the baby would ever come.
Then, one snowy night at dinner, the phone rang. Mom listened, and her hand went to her mouth.
"A baby girl was born today," she said. "Her name is Ruby." The three of them hugged in the middle of the kitchen.
They packed in twenty minutes flat: the car seat, a suitcase, diapers and, of course, Eli's camera.
Ruby had been born in another state, so they drove through the night. Eli watched the highway lights until his eyes closed.
At sunrise they pulled up at the hospital, tired and nervous and excited all at once.
A nurse placed Ruby in Mom's arms. She had a full head of dark hair and the tiniest fingernails Eli had ever seen.
Then it was Eli's turn. He sat very still while Dad helped him hold his sister for the first time.
Eli took his first photo of the three of them. Then a nurse took one of all four.
They could not go home yet. For a week they lived in a hotel room, waiting for the adoption papers to be finished.
In that hotel room Eli learned to test a bottle on his wrist and to burp Ruby over his shoulder.
Every afternoon they pushed Ruby's stroller around the snowy park next to the hotel.
On the seventh day the papers were ready. Mom and Dad signed their names, and Eli gave a double thumbs-up.
They flew home. Ruby slept on Dad's chest the whole flight while Eli photographed the clouds.
At home the neighbors had hung a giant banner across the porch, and everyone came out to wave.
Grandma arrived with a quilt she had sewn all year, with a square for every person in the family.
That night Eli gave Ruby her first bath at home, with Dad holding her head and Eli holding the washcloth.
Eli glued every photo of the trip into an album. He called it The Day Ruby Came Home.

pages.intro: Dinosaurs are one of the most searched coloring themes, and a dinosaur adventure story coloring book adds a plot that keeps kids turning pages instead of skipping around. Here are five 24-page story books, each with one story from start to finish: a lost triceratops finding her herd, a boy hiding a hatchling, a young pteranodon learning to fly, a brachiosaurus baker and a summer fossil dig. tips: Name each dinosaur species in the brief so the pages draw a real triceratops or ankylosaurus, not a generic dino.

pageTexts: Trixie was the smallest triceratops in the herd. Every morning she splashed in the river while her mother drank beside her.
One afternoon a thunderstorm crashed over the valley. The herd ran for shelter, and Trixie hid under a big fern.
When the rain stopped, the valley was quiet. Trixie looked all around, but her herd was gone.
Trixie took a deep breath. "I will find them," she said, and she set off on her short, strong legs.
On a tall cliff sat a pteranodon. "Have you seen my herd?" Trixie called up.
"I saw big dinosaurs walking that way," said the pteranodon, and it pointed to the fern forest.
In the fern forest Trixie found footprints so big she could stand inside one. She followed them, step by step.
The footprints belonged to a kind brachiosaurus. "Your herd went toward the river," she said softly.
Stomp, stomp! The ground began to shake. Trixie hid behind a fallen log and kept very still.
A big T. rex wandered past, yawning a giant yawn. It never saw Trixie at all.
At last Trixie reached the river, but it was wide and fast. How could a little triceratops get across?
A diplodocus was wading nearby. "Hop on," it said, and it laid its long tail across the water like a bridge.
Trixie walked along the tail, one careful step at a time, all the way to the other side.
By now Trixie was very hungry. She found a bush full of juicy berries, just out of reach.
A parasaurolophus family pulled the berries down for her. "Share with us," they said, and they all ate together.
The baby parasaurolophus blew through its crest. Toot, toot! Trixie laughed so hard her frill wiggled.
Further on, smoke puffed from a far-off volcano. An ankylosaurus stood on the path. "Wait here with me until it clears," he said.
They sat under a rock ledge and told each other stories while the smoke drifted by.
Soon the sky was clear again. "Good luck, little one," said the ankylosaurus, and Trixie trotted on.
Trixie climbed a tall hill. It was steep, but she kept going, up and up and up.
From the top she could see the whole valley. And there, by the river, was her herd!
Trixie ran down the hill as fast as her legs could go.
Her mother saw her and came running. She nuzzled Trixie's nose and held her close.
The herd circled round, happy to have Trixie home. That night she slept safe and warm beside her mother.

pageTexts: Owen was hunting for a fishing net in Grandpa's shed when he found something strange: a big speckled egg in a bucket of straw.
He carried it to his room, wrapped it in socks and set it under his desk lamp to keep it warm.
Crack! Out popped a baby ankylosaurus with a bumpy back and a tiny club on the end of its tail.
"I'll call you Clunk," Owen whispered, because that was the sound his tail made on the floor.
Owen kept Clunk a secret. The first week he hid him in the laundry basket, right under Mom's nose.
Clunk grew fast. By the second week he only fit in the bathtub, and he loved the bubbles.
Soon the bathtub was too small, so Owen wheeled Clunk out to the yard in Grandpa's wheelbarrow.
For a few days Clunk lived in the treehouse, until he was too big to turn around.
Now Clunk was as big as a pony. Owen built him a tent from a tarp and brought him apples every day.
One morning Clunk ate every one of Grandpa's tomato plants. "Clunk!" groaned Owen.
The next day Clunk chased the mail truck all the way down the street. Letters flew everywhere.
Then he spotted the birdbath. Swing, smash! Clunk's tail was a lot stronger than it used to be.
Owen swept up the pieces. Clunk hung his head. "You can't help being a dinosaur," Owen sighed.
On Monday Owen walked to the school bus stop, and Clunk followed him there.
"Hide!" Owen said, pushing Clunk into the hedge. The bus driver scratched his head.
That night Owen read his dinosaur book to Clunk. Ankylosaurs lived in warm swamps, it said, long ago. Clunk looked homesick.
The next morning Grandpa lifted the tarp. He looked at Clunk. He looked at Owen. Then he started to smile.
"So that's where my egg went," said Grandpa. "Come with me. I have a secret too."
Behind the boxes was a door that glowed. Grandpa opened it, and warm air rushed in.
On the other side was a steamy swamp full of giant ferns and dragonflies as big as birds.
Out of the reeds came a family of ankylosaurs. Clunk lifted his head and gave a happy rumble.
Owen hugged Clunk goodbye. Clunk nudged a smooth round stone into his hand, like a present.
Back home, Owen put the stone beside the eggshell on Grandpa's shelf. "Can we visit him?" he asked. Grandpa winked.
That night Owen fell asleep with the stone in his hand, dreaming of a little dinosaur splashing in a faraway swamp.

Wren landing on the cliff ledge beside the nest while her mother and her brothers and sisters crowd around her, flapping their wings with joy.

pageTexts: High on a sea cliff lived a family of pteranodons. Wren, the smallest, had a crooked crest and wings that would not lift her.
One by one her brothers and sisters jumped off the ledge and soared away. Wren stayed behind.
Every day Wren practiced. Flap, flap, flap! But her feet never left the rock.
One windy morning she tried a big jump. Down, down, down she tumbled.
Splash! Wren landed in the sea. Then something big rose up underneath her.
It was a plesiosaur with a long, long neck. "Up you come," it said, and it carried her to a rock.
Wren spread her wings to dry in the sun. "Don't give up," called the plesiosaur as it swam away.
So Wren climbed all the way back up the cliff, claw over claw, ledge by ledge.
She stood at the edge, spread her wings wide and jumped. This time the wind caught her!
Wren was flying! She glided along the coast, looking down at the whole wide world.
She flew over a beach where duck-billed dinosaurs were sitting on their nests of eggs.
At the river mouth, a herd of triceratops looked up and waved their tails as she went by.
Wren was tired, so she rested on the head of a sauropod wading in a lagoon. It didn't mind at all.
On a sandbar a T. rex looked up and snapped its jaws. Wren flapped higher, far out of reach.
She flew past a smoking volcano island, where the air was warm and smelled of ash.
Then dark clouds rolled in. Rain lashed down and the wind pushed Wren this way and that.
Wren remembered the wind at the cliff. She found a rising draft of warm air and rode it up, up, up through the storm.
Above the clouds the sky was calm. Below her, the storm drifted away and a rainbow appeared.
Now Wren was hungry. Down below she spotted a shining school of fish.
She folded her wings and dove, straight as an arrow.
Splash! When she came up, a fish was wriggling in her beak. Her very first catch!
As the sun went down, Wren flew home along the coast with her fish.
Her family was waiting on the ledge. "You flew!" they cried, crowding around her.
The next morning, the whole family flew out over the sea together, and Wren, the smallest, led the way.

pageTexts: At the top of Fern Valley there was a bakery, and the baker was Bronte the brachiosaurus.
Bronte's oven was very high up, but her long neck reached it easily.
Today was little Stego's birthday, so Bronte mixed the biggest bowl of batter she had ever made.
She baked seven cake layers and stacked them up, one on top of another, into a volcano cake.
She drizzled frosting down the sides like lava and added candles on the top.
Bronte packed the cake into her wagon with bread, muffins, buns and pies, and off she went.
First she stopped at the farm. "A fresh loaf for the farmers!" The triceratops cheered.
Next came the ankylosaurus road crew, fixing the bumpy path. Bronte gave them warm muffins.
At the mail hut, the pteranodon mail carriers swooped down for sticky buns.
At the stream Bronte lifted the cake high on her head and stepped across, stone by stone.
By the lake, the duck-billed dinosaurs were having a picnic. Bronte brought them two big pies.
Then the sky grew dark. "Oh no," said Bronte. "Not rain, not today!"
Down came the rain. Bronte bent her long neck over the cake, but the rain kept coming.
Then a big T. rex stepped out of the trees and held a giant leaf over the cake. "I'll help," he said.
Together they walked through the rain, splashing in every puddle, and the cake stayed dry.
Soon the rain stopped and a rainbow came out. "Thank you!" Bronte called as the T. rex waved goodbye.
Bronte hurried on with the wagon. Stego's party was about to begin.
There was Stego's house, with balloons on the door and flags on the roof. Bronte was just in time!
Stego opened the door and gasped. "A volcano cake! For me?"
Bronte set the cake on the table, and all of Stego's friends gathered round.
Everyone from the valley came: the farmers, the road crew, the mail carriers, the picnickers and the kind T. rex. They all sang "Happy Birthday" to Stego.
Stego made a wish and blew out all the candles with one big puff.
Then everyone had a slice. It was the best cake in all of Fern Valley.
When the party was over, Bronte pulled her empty wagon home under the stars, happy and tired.

prompts.name: Sora's summer fossil dig
