pageTexts: Sora was eleven the summer her aunt, a paleontologist, took her to a fossil dig in the badlands of Montana.
They set up camp between the striped hills, with tents, a camp stove and enough water for weeks.
Her aunt showed her the tools: rock hammers, brushes, dental picks and a notebook for writing down everything.
Each morning they hiked the dry gullies, eyes on the ground, looking for anything that was not just rock.
On the fourth day Sora spotted it: a round, weathered bone poking out of a hill. A vertebra!
Her aunt studied it through her lens and grinned. "This is a big one. Let's get the team."
First they mapped the site, with string and stakes, so every bone could be recorded exactly where it lay.
Then came the slow part: brushing away the rock, a little at a time, for days.
Slowly a giant hip bone appeared, wider than Sora's arms could reach.
Next came a leg bone. Sora lay down beside it. It was as long as she was.
At noon it was too hot to dig, so they ate lunch in the shade and guessed what the dinosaur might be.
Then, under a rock ledge, Sora brushed away the dust and found a horn. Then another, and another. It was a triceratops skull!
That night by the campfire, her aunt explained how triceratops lived here 66 million years ago, when this dry land was a green river plain.
In her tent Sora dreamed of the herd walking across a warm, green land, right where she was sleeping.
To move the bones safely, they wrapped each one in burlap soaked in plaster, like a cast for a broken arm.
One afternoon a hailstorm swept in. The team held a tarp over the jackets while hailstones bounced all around.
When it passed, the gully was running with muddy water, but every jacket was safe.
The skull jacket was too heavy to carry out, so a helicopter came and lifted it over the hills.
They loaded every jacket onto a flatbed truck, packed up camp and drove the bones to the museum.
In the museum lab, preparators spent months cleaning the bones, grain by grain, with tiny air-powered tools.
Sora came back to help on weekends, sorting small fragments and gluing broken pieces back together.
At last the skeleton was ready to stand. The team built a steel frame and raised it piece by piece.
On opening day, hundreds of people came to see the triceratops that Sora found.
Sora stood beneath it and read the sign: Discovered by Sora, age eleven. She was already planning next summer's dig.

pages.title: Space Adventure Story Coloring Book Prompts
pages.metaDescription: Space story coloring book prompts: five 24-page books written page by page, from a teapot rocket to the Moon to a Mars dust storm rescue.
pages.intro: A space adventure story coloring book turns the solar system into a journey, with a new planet, moon or rescue every few pages. Here are five story coloring books of 24 pages each: a mouse flying a teapot rocket to the Moon, a race to every planet, an alien visitor on a farm, a twelve-year-old saving the greenhouse on Mars and a comet delivering mail to the moons. They suit space-mad children, teachers adding a story to a science unit and KDP sellers in the space niche. Each book is written out page by page, with the picture and the words for every page, so you can paste one page at a time into ChatGPT, Gemini or any AI image tool.
keywords: space story coloring book for kids
tips: Make each stop a real place (the Moon, Mars, Saturn's rings, Europa) so the book teaches a little while it tells the story.
A 24-page planet tour has room for every planet plus takeoff and landing; list the stops in order in the brief.
Bring the hero home on the last pages; a trip that returns feels finished.

prompts.name: Luna-Mae's teapot rocket to the Moon
prompts.brief: Luna-Mae, a small mouse in a knitted helmet, wants to know if the Moon is made of cheese. In 24 pages she builds a rocket from a teapot, a thimble and two spoons, blasts off from the kitchen windowsill, floats past clouds, a satellite and a sleepy comet, lands in a crater, bounces in low gravity, finds old astronaut footprints and a parked moon buggy, digs in the dust, watches Earth rise and licks a moon rock: not cheese. She flies home, lands in the sugar bowl and has cheese on toast for supper.
prompts.why: Parents of preschoolers get a funny 24-page first trip to the Moon with real lunar sights and a cozy ending at home.

pageTexts: Luna-Mae the mouse looked up at the big round Moon. "I think it is made of cheese," she said.
She could not stop wondering. There was only one way to find out for sure.
She found an old teapot, a silver thimble and two shiny spoons.
She tied on the spoons for fins and put the thimble on top. Her rocket was ready!
Luna-Mae put on her knitted helmet and packed a cracker for the trip.
She climbed in and counted down. Three, two, one...
Whoosh! The teapot rocket blasted off out of the window.
Up she flew, past the fluffy clouds and one very surprised bird.
She waved to a satellite turning slowly in the dark.
A sleepy comet gave a big yawn as she zoomed by.
Inside the rocket, Luna-Mae floated upside down. Her cracker crumbs floated too!
The Moon grew bigger and bigger. It was covered in round holes.
Bump! The rocket landed in a big round crater.
Luna-Mae climbed down and made her very first tiny footprint.
On the Moon she could jump so high! Boing, boing, boing!
She found giant old footprints. Someone had been here before!
Next to them was a parked moon buggy. She sat in the big seat and pretended to drive.
She dug in the dust with a spoon. It did not smell like cheese at all.
Then she saw Earth rising over the edge of the Moon. Home looked beautiful.
At last she licked a moon rock. Yuck! The Moon is not made of cheese.
Luna-Mae laughed, climbed back into her rocket and flew home.
Plop! She landed right in the sugar bowl.
For supper she had cheese on toast. Earth cheese is the best cheese of all.
That night the Moon shone in at her window, and Luna-Mae smiled in her sleep.

prompts.name: Kofi and Bolt's solar system rally
prompts.brief: Kofi, eight, and his robot dog Bolt enter the Great Planet Rally: visit every planet, collect a stamp at each and get back to Earth first. pageTexts: Kofi, eight, and his robot dog Bolt signed up for the Great Planet Rally: visit every planet, get a stamp at each and be the first one home.
On race day, rockets lined up on the school field. Kofi and Bolt climbed into theirs.
Three, two, one, go! The rockets roared up into the sky.
First stop was Mercury, closest to the Sun. It was so hot that Bolt's metal ears steamed.
A stamp robot stamped their card. One planet down, plenty more to go.
At Venus they dipped under thick, swirling clouds and spotted volcanoes far below.
On Mars a huge dust storm chased them across the rocks. Kofi steered as fast as he could.
They grabbed the Mars stamp beside a giant volcano just before the dust rolled in.
Next came the asteroid belt. Kofi zigzagged between the tumbling rocks.
A zippy saucer flown by a girl named Mira whizzed past. "See you at the finish!" she called.
Jupiter was enormous. Its Great Red Spot is a storm bigger than the whole Earth.
A stamp drone met them beside Jupiter's moons. Stamp!
At Saturn, Kofi slid the rocket along the rings, past chunks of ice as big as houses.
Bolt leaned out on his safety line and caught a little ice chunk, like a game of fetch.
Uranus spins on its side. Kofi tipped his head to see it the right way up.
Neptune has the fastest winds of all. They shoved the rocket this way and that.
Then Bolt's battery ran out. The lights flickered and went dark.
Kofi found the backup pedal power and pedaled with all his might.
Bolt beeped back to life, and they got the last stamp at Neptune.
On the way home they waved to little Pluto with its heart-shaped plain.
They raced back toward Earth. Mira's saucer was just ahead.
Mira landed first. Kofi and Bolt came in second.
Then the judge checked the cards. Only Kofi's had a stamp from every planet.
Kofi and Bolt won the Explorer's Cup, and Mira asked if they could fly the rally together next year.

prompts.name: Blip the alien lands on Grandma's farm
prompts.brief: Blip, a small alien with three antennae and a round saucer ship, crash-lands in Grandma Rose's cornfield. pageTexts: One night a little round spaceship wobbled down from the stars toward Grandma Rose's farm.
Bump! It landed in the cornfield with a bent leg and a puff of smoke.
In the morning, twins Ava and Sam found it. Out peeked Blip, a little alien with three antennae.
"Hello," said Ava. "Blip," said Blip, and waved all three antennae.
They showed Blip a cow. "Moo!" Blip jumped right up in the air.
In the chicken coop, a hen sat on Blip's head like a hat.
Grandma Rose gave them a bumpy ride on the big tractor.
They found a big muddy puddle. Splash! Blip loved puddles.
Sam picked Blip an apple off the tree. Crunch! Blip's eyes went wide.
The piglets snuffled Blip's toes, and he giggled and giggled.
They played hide and seek. Blip hid well, except for his antennae.
Before bed they lay on the grass, and Blip pointed to the tiny star that was his home.
At bath time Blip tried bubbles for the very first time.
At bedtime Grandma read a story, and Blip's antennae glowed like night-lights.
In the morning Blip looked at his broken ship and then at the sky. He wanted to go home.
"We can fix it," said Grandma Rose, and she fetched her toolbox, a colander and her sewing kit.
Sam and Blip fitted a tractor part where the bent leg had been.
Ava put the colander on top as a brand-new antenna dish.
Grandma Rose sewed a neat patch over a tear in the seat.
Blip pressed the buttons. The ship hummed and lifted off the ground!
It was time to say goodbye. Grandma gave Blip a basket of apples for the trip.
At sunset Blip lifted off, and all the farm animals watched him go.
That night the twins saw a new star blinking at them from the sky.
Far away, Blip munched an apple, blinked his ship's light and said goodnight to his friends.

prompts.name: Tessa and the Mars dust storm
prompts.brief: Tessa, twelve, with a shaved head and a patched jumpsuit, is one of the first kids living at Ares Base on Mars. In 24 pages the book shows her days: exercise in low gravity, school over video from Earth, tomatoes in the greenhouse dome, the rover ride to the ice mine, blue Martian sunsets. Then a dust storm buries the solar farm, the grown-ups are stuck at the mine and the greenhouse starts to freeze. Tessa and her friend Dev drive the rover through the storm, dig out the panels, reroute a snapped cable and get the heaters running. When the dust clears, the base eats the first ripe tomatoes.
prompts.why: Older space fans and STEM teachers get a 24-page story of daily life on Mars with a rescue that runs on real Martian dangers.

Tessa and her friend Dev at a desk in the base school room watching a teacher on a big video screen, tablets and headsets on the desk.
Tessa in the greenhouse dome watering rows of tomato plants under hanging grow lights, plastic pipes and nearly ripe tomatoes all around.
Tessa and Dev in the airlock pulling on pressure suits and locking their clear-visor helmets, suit racks and a hatch wheel behind them.
A big six-wheeled rover bouncing across rocky dunes, Tessa driving with Chief Engineer Okafor beside her and Dev in the back seat.
Inside the ice mine, Dev drilling blocks of ice from a tunnel wall while Tessa loads them onto a cart with rails.
Tessa and Dev sitting on the rover's roof at dusk watching a small sun set over the crater rim, a glow spreading around it.
Tessa standing in the base control room staring at a big weather screen showing a huge swirling storm moving toward the base.
A towering wall of dust swallowing the domes of Ares Base, the outside lights glowing faintly through the swirling sand.
Rows of solar panels half buried under drifts of dust, a power meter dial inside the base dropping close to empty.
Tessa touching a frosty tomato leaf in the cold greenhouse, frost patterns spreading across the dome glass and the heaters switched off.
Tessa and Dev at the radio console talking to Chief Okafor on a small screen, the grown-ups sheltering in the ice mine tunnel.
Tessa and Dev leaning over a base map spread on a table, a flashlight on it and a finger tracing the path to the solar farm.
The rover driving into the storm, its headlights cutting through the dust, a row of tall marker poles leading the way.
Dev digging sand from around a sunken rover wheel with a shovel while Tessa holds up a big lamp, dust whirling around them.
Tessa and Dev arriving at the solar farm, only the tops of the panels poking out of the dust drifts in long rows.
Tessa and Dev sweeping dust off a solar panel with wide brooms, the wind blowing their safety lines sideways.
Tessa kneeling at an open junction box rerouting a thick cable to a spare socket with a wrench, a snapped cable end beside her.
Small status lights shining on top of the cleared solar panels as Dev throws his arms up in a cheer beside the rover.
Back in the greenhouse, Tessa holding a tomato plant up to a warm heater as the frost drips off the leaves, Dev pulling off his helmet.
The dust thinning over the base as the sun shows again, the rover with the grown-ups driving home from the ice mine.
Chief Engineer Okafor pinning round badges with a lightning bolt onto Tessa's and Dev's jumpsuits, the crew clapping around them.
The whole base crew gathered at a long table in the greenhouse dome, sharing a bowl of the first ripe tomatoes, Tessa holding one up.
pageTexts: Tessa is twelve, and she is one of the first kids to live on Mars, at a place called Ares Base.
Every day starts with exercise, because Mars gravity is weak and muscles get lazy fast.
School comes over video from Earth. Messages take up to twenty minutes to arrive, so questions have to wait.
After school Tessa looks after the tomatoes in the greenhouse dome. They are almost ripe.
To go outside, Tessa and Dev suit up in the airlock. The air on Mars is far too thin to breathe.
They ride the six-wheeled rover out to the ice mine with Chief Engineer Okafor.
Ice dug from under the ground gives the base its water and the air everyone breathes.
On Mars the sunsets glow blue. Tessa and Dev never get tired of them.
One evening the weather screen showed a giant dust storm rolling toward the base.
By morning the storm had swallowed the sky. Dust hid the sun completely.
Dust buried the solar farm, and the base's power began to fall.
Without power the greenhouse heaters stopped. Frost crept over the tomato leaves.
The grown-ups were stuck at the ice mine until the storm passed. Someone had to save the greenhouse.
Tessa and Dev knew the path to the solar farm by heart. They made a plan.
They drove the rover into the storm, following the marker poles one by one.
A wheel sank into soft sand. Dev dug it out while Tessa held the lamp.
At the solar farm, only the tops of the panels poked out of the dust.
They brushed and shoveled, panel after panel, while the wind howled.
A cable had snapped. Tessa rerouted it to a spare socket, just like she had practiced.
The lights on the panels blinked on. Power was flowing again!
Back at base the heaters hummed, and the frost melted from the tomatoes.
Days later the dust cleared, and the grown-ups drove home from the ice mine.
Chief Okafor pinned a Storm Crew badge on Tessa and on Dev.
That night the whole base ate the first ripe tomatoes on Mars, and they tasted like home.

prompts.name: Zip the comet postman
prompts.brief: Zip, a young comet with a long ice tail, a postman's cap and a mailbag, delivers post around the solar system in 24 pages. He loops out from the Sun to the craters of Mercury and Earth's Moon, sorts letters on Mars's tiny moon Phobos, rings a bell on volcanic Io, skates over the ice of Europa, lunches on Saturn's rings, leaves a package under Titan's haze, dodges the geysers of Enceladus and visits Miranda's giant cliff and icy Triton. The last letter has no address. Zip follows the clues past Pluto and delivers it to a lonely rock, then turns for home.
prompts.why: Kids who already know the planets get 24 pages of real moons, and teachers get a story they can use alongside a lesson on the outer solar system.

Zip holding out the envelope to the little rock, who reaches for it with tiny stubby arms and a hopeful smile.
The little rock holding up a card with a drawing of the smiling Sun on it, Zip beaming beside it.

Zip zooming back toward the far-off Sun with his tail lighting up the dark, the little rock waving goodbye behind him.
pageTexts: Zip is a young comet with a long icy tail, and he is the postman of the solar system.
Every morning he puts on his cap and fills his mailbag with postcards and parcels.
Off he zooms, looping away from the Sun with his tail shining behind him.
First stop is Mercury. Zip drops off a parcel of sun hats at the hot, rocky craters.
Next he visits Earth's Moon and pops a postcard into the crater mailbox.
On Phobos, Mars's tiny lumpy moon, he stops to sort his letters.
He weaves through the asteroid belt, holding his mailbag tight.
On Io, volcanoes puff and bubble. Zip rings the doorbell and hands over a parcel.
On Europa he skates over the cracked ice and slips a letter down to the ocean below.
At Saturn he sits on the rings for lunch and watches the ice drift by.
Under Titan's thick, hazy sky, he leaves a package beside a quiet lake.
On Enceladus, icy geysers shoot into space. Zip holds his mailbag high to keep it dry.
He delivers a postcard to the tallest cliff in the solar system, on Uranus's moon Miranda.
Far out at icy Triton, Neptune's biggest moon, he posts the last letter on his list.
But one letter is left at the bottom of the bag, and it has no address at all.
On the back is a little drawing: a round rock and a dotted path leading past Pluto.
Pluto and its moon Charon point the way. "Out there, past everything," they say.
He flies on into the cold, dark Kuiper Belt, where the Sun looks like a tiny star.
His tail glows like a lantern as he checks rock after rock.
At last he finds a small round rock sitting all alone.
"This is for you," says Zip. The little rock has never had a letter before.
It is a card from the Sun, who can see every rock, even the far-away ones. It says you are not forgotten.
The rock writes a reply straight away, and Zip tucks it into his bag.
Then Zip turns for home, his tail lighting up the dark behind him.

pages.title: Kindness and Friendship Story Coloring Book Prompts
pages.theme: Kindness and Friendship Story Coloring Book
pages.metaDescription: Kindness and friendship story coloring book prompts: five 24-page stories written page by page, from a prickly porcupine to two science fair rivals.
pages.intro: These kindness and friendship story coloring books are for children from preschool to middle school, the teachers who use them in social-emotional lessons and the parents who use them to talk about friends and sharing. There are five 24-page stories: a porcupine whose quills get in the way of hugs, a girl doing one kind act for every house on her block, two new friends who share no language, a rain cloud who gives her rain away, and two eleven-year-old rivals building a solar oven. Each book is written out page by page, a picture and a line or two of story for every page, so you can paste one page at a time into ChatGPT, Gemini or any AI image tool.
tips: Show kindness as small, copyable actions (carrying groceries, sharing a ball) on their own pages.
A 24-page story gives a friendship time to grow; show the first meeting, a few setbacks and the day they become friends.
Teachers buy these for SEL lessons; a book with one scene per page gives the class something to talk about on every page.

prompts.name: Pickle the porcupine wants a hug
prompts.brief: A 24-page story. Pickle, a young porcupine with a green scarf, moves to Maple Meadow and wants a friend, but her quills get in the way: she pops the rabbits' balloons, gets stuck in the squirrels' tug-of-war rope and pricks Mole at a picnic. She tries a pillow, a pot and a coat of leaves. Then she rolls up the apples after a windstorm, holds up the frogs' tent in the rain and carries paper lanterns for the meadow party. There an old tortoise gives her the first hug, and everyone else hugs her in oven mitts.
prompts.why: Parents and preschool teachers get a funny 24-page friendship story where the hero's odd trait ends up helping the whole meadow.

Pickle standing tall in the middle of the frogs' tent, her quills holding up the roof like a pole, the frogs dry inside sipping from mugs.
The meadow animals making paper lanterns at a long table, Mole holding up a lantern and scratching his head, a tall tree with bare branches behind.
Pickle walking under the tree with paper lanterns spiked on every quill while squirrels take them off and hang them on the branches.
An evening party under lantern-hung trees, tables of pies and lemonade, an old tortoise with a big patterned shell walking slowly up to Pickle.
The old tortoise and Pickle in a big hug, his hard shell pressed against her quills, both smiling, a lantern glowing above them.
All the meadow animals wearing oven mitts on their paws in one big group hug around Pickle, lanterns in the trees and a full moon above.
pageTexts: Pickle the porcupine pulled her little wagon into Maple Meadow. "I hope I make a friend here," she said.
Her new home was a cozy burrow under the old oak tree. Pickle unpacked her teacups and wished for someone to share them with.
Over the hedge, the rabbits were having a balloon party. Pickle hurried over to say hello.
She gave the biggest rabbit a hug. Pop! Pop! Pop! Every balloon burst on her quills.
"Sorry," said Pickle, and her nose drooped. The rabbits said it was all right, but the party was very quiet after that.
Next she found the squirrels playing tug-of-war. "I can pull!" said Pickle, and she grabbed the rope.
The rope stuck fast in her quills. The squirrels tumbled into a heap, and nobody could get the rope out.
At the picnic, Pickle sat down close to Mole. "Ouch!" said Mole, and he jumped right off the blanket.
That night Pickle sat alone on a log. "Everyone runs away from my prickles," she sighed.
In the morning she had a plan. She tied her fluffiest pillow onto her back.
But the pillow caught on a bramble and burst. Feathers floated all over the meadow.
Then she tried a big cooking pot. Clank, clonk, clank! It was much too noisy for hugging.
Last she covered her quills with leaves. A deer tried to nibble her, because she looked just like a bush!
Pickle shook off every leaf. "Maybe I can't stop being prickly," she said. "But maybe I can be prickly and kind."
That afternoon a great wind blew through Maple Meadow. Apples tumbled from every tree in the orchard.
Pickle curled up and rolled through the grass. The apples stuck to her quills, ten at a time!
She filled every basket in the meadow. "Thank you, Pickle!" cheered the rabbits and the squirrels.
Then the rain came, and the frogs' tent pole snapped. The wet tent sagged down onto their heads.
Pickle stood up tall in the middle. Her quills held the tent up, and the frogs stayed warm and dry.
Everyone was getting ready for the meadow party. "How will we hang all these lanterns?" asked Mole.
Pickle carried twenty lanterns on her quills at once, and the squirrels hung them on every branch.
At the party, an old tortoise came slowly up to Pickle. "My shell is very hard," he said with a smile.
He gave her a great big hug, and nothing poked at all. It was Pickle's very first hug in Maple Meadow.
Then the rabbits, the squirrels, Mole and the frogs put on oven mitts, and everybody hugged Pickle at once!

prompts.name: Amara's neighborhood kindness map
prompts.brief: A 24-page story. Amara, seven, with braids tied in beads, draws a map of her block and plans one kind thing for every house in a single Saturday. She carries Mrs. Kim's groceries, waters Mr. Lopez's tomatoes, chalks a hopscotch for the twins, walks a puppy for a man on crutches, returns a lost cat, leaves a drawing for the mail carrier, bakes muffins with her mom for the fire station and reads to a neighbor at the senior home. By evening every house has a star, and the whole block surprises her with a street picnic at sunset.
prompts.why: Teachers and parents get a 24-page book of real, copyable kind acts in a real neighborhood, with a clear one-act-per-house structure.

pageTexts: On Saturday morning, Amara drew a map of her whole block. There were eight houses on it, and she knew someone in every one.
"Today I'm going to do one kind thing for every house," she told Mom. "Each time I do one, I'll draw a star."
She tucked the map in her pocket and stepped outside. The street was sunny and still a little sleepy.
Next door, Mrs. Kim was looking at six heavy bags of groceries. "I can carry those," said Amara.
They carried every bag up the steps together. Mrs. Kim gave her a clementine, and Amara drew her first star.
Mr. Lopez's back was sore, and his tomatoes were thirsty. Amara watered every plant down the row.
"The best tomato is yours," said Mr. Lopez. Star number two went on the map.
The twins at the yellow house were bored. Amara chalked the longest hopscotch on the whole street.
Soon all three of them were hopping and laughing. The twins added chalk flowers, and Amara added star number three.
Mr. Osei had a broken leg and a puppy who wanted to run. "May I walk him for you?" asked Amara.
Biscuit the puppy pulled her all the way around the block and back again. Star number four!
In the park, Amara spotted a fluffy cat hiding under a bench. It looked just like the picture on the lamppost.
She carried the cat home to the blue house. Its owner hugged it tight, and Amara drew star number five.
At lunch, Amara drew a picture of the mail carrier, who walks their block in sun, rain and snow.
She left it in the mailbox with a thank-you note. When he found it, he smiled all the way down the street. Star six!
In the afternoon, Amara and Mom baked two dozen blueberry muffins. Amara got flour on her nose.
They carried the muffins to the fire station on the corner. "Thank you for keeping our block safe," said Amara.
The firefighters let her sit in the big truck and try on a helmet. Star number seven went on the map.
Her last stop was the senior home at the end of the street. Amara read Mrs. Petrova her favorite book about the sea.
Then Mrs. Petrova taught Amara how to knit one whole row. Star number eight!
As the sun went down, Amara sat on her stoop and looked at her map. Every house had a star.
Then she heard chairs scraping. All her neighbors were carrying tables and food into the street.
"Surprise!" called Mrs. Kim. "You were kind to all of us today, so now it's our turn."
That night Amara drew one more star, the biggest of all, right in the middle of the map, for the whole block.

prompts.name: Yusuf and June's recess game
prompts.brief: A 24-page story over one school week. Yusuf, eight, has just arrived from far away and speaks no English yet; he wears a knit cap and carries a worn soccer ball. June, eight, has short hair and a cast on her arm, so she can't play tag at recess. On Monday Yusuf shows her a game with a ball and five stones. Through the week they teach each other words with drawings and pointing: ball, sun, lunch, sister, funny. They swap lunches, make up a handshake, get lost on a field trip and find their way back. On Friday they teach the stone game to the whole class.
prompts.why: Teachers with new-to-English students and families who've moved get a 24-page school-week friendship story built on actions, not words.

A big tiered fountain ahead of them, the teacher hurrying toward the two children with her arms out and the class waving beside the bus.

Yusuf and June at the front of the classroom on Friday holding up the five stones and the soccer ball while the class leans forward.
The whole class sitting in a circle on the playground while Yusuf bounces the ball and June shows how to scoop a stone one-handed.

pageTexts: On Monday, Yusuf came to a new school in a new country. He didn't know a single word of English yet.
The teacher said his name, and the class waved. Yusuf held his cap tight and waved back.
At recess, June sat on the bench. Her arm was in a cast, so she couldn't play tag.
Yusuf sat down at the other end of the bench. Neither of them said anything, because neither knew what to say.
Then Yusuf picked up five smooth stones and set them in a row. He bounced his ball and scooped up a stone before he caught it.
June tried it with her good hand. Bounce, scoop, catch! Yusuf clapped, and June laughed out loud.
On Tuesday, June brought a notebook. She drew a ball, pointed and said, "Ball." Yusuf said, "Ball!"
Yusuf drew a sun and said the word in his language. June tried it, and he grinned at the way she said it.
On Wednesday they learned "lunch," and then they swapped. June loved the flatbread. Yusuf loved the sandwich.
Yusuf drew a girl with pigtails. "Sister," said June, and she drew her baby brother in his high chair.
Then June made her silliest face. "Funny!" she said. Yusuf laughed so hard he nearly fell off the bench.
They made up a secret handshake: a thumb hook, a wiggle and a gentle bump on June's cast.
Yusuf drew a sun and a soccer ball on June's cast. June said it was the best drawing on it.
On Thursday, the class took a bus to the city park. Yusuf and June shared a seat by the window.
They stopped to watch a line of ducklings. When they looked up, the class was gone.
The paths all looked the same. June's tummy went tight, and Yusuf held his ball close.
June opened the notebook and drew the bus beside the big fountain. Yusuf nodded and pointed at the sun.
They walked toward the sun, past the roses and around the hedges, checking June's map as they went.
There was the fountain, and there was their teacher running to meet them. "You found your way back!" she said.
On the bus home they were so tired they fell asleep, still holding the notebook and the ball.
On Friday, the teacher asked if they had something to share. Yusuf and June looked at each other and nodded.
At recess, Yusuf showed everyone the stone game, and June showed them how to play it with just one hand.
Soon the whole playground was bouncing and scooping. Even the tag players wanted a turn.
At the end of the day, Yusuf said his first English sentence: "June is my friend." June said it back in his language.

pageTexts: Puff was a little round cloud with a curl on top. One summer morning, she woke up over a sunny valley.
It was a very hot day. The sun shone and shone, and everything in the valley felt thirsty.
A tired cow was lying in the hot field. Puff floated over her and made a big, cool shadow.
"Moo, thank you!" said the cow, and she munched her grass in the shade.
Next Puff saw a vegetable garden. The carrots and cabbages were droopy and dry.
Puff rained a gentle rain, pitter-patter. The cabbages perked right up. Puff got a little bit smaller.
In the town, a little dog was panting on the hot sidewalk. His water bowl was empty.
Puff sprinkled cool drops on his back and filled his bowl to the top. The little dog wagged and wagged.
Three little birds sat on an empty bird bath. "No splashing today," they peeped.
Puff filled it to the brim. Splish, splash! The birds had the best bath ever. Puff got smaller again.
Over the hill was a field of sunflowers with their big heads hanging low.
Puff rained and rained until every sunflower stood up tall and turned its face to the sky.
Down below, the wind blew the farmer's bonfire toward his haystack. His little bucket was not enough.
Puff squeezed out a big shower. Whoosh! The fire went out in a puff of steam, and the farmer cheered.
Now Puff was not round at all. She was just a tiny wisp floating over the lake.
"I gave all my rain away," she whispered. "Now I'm too small to help anyone."
But the lake had been watching. It breathed up soft, curly mist, all the way to Puff.
The mist joined Puff, and she grew rounder and rounder. Her curl popped back up on top.
Then the wind came whistling over the hills. "Puff! I brought your friends!" it called.
Big clouds and little clouds floated in to meet her, long ones and tall ones and bumpy ones.
Together they made one big, fluffy cloud family, and Puff was the biggest she had ever been.
They rained a soft, happy rain over the whole valley, on the cow, the garden and the sunflowers.
Then the sun peeked out from behind Puff, and its light sparkled in every raindrop.
A great big rainbow stretched across the valley. "Thank you, Puff!" called everyone she had helped.

prompts.name: Maya and Dev's science fair

A busy school gym science fair with rows of project tables, Maya pointing to a chart and Dev to the mirrors while two judges taste pizza.

pageTexts: Maya and Dev were both sure they were the best at science in Room 12. They had never agreed on anything.
Then Ms. Okafor drew names for science fair partners. "Maya and Dev," she read. Both of them groaned.
Maya wanted to test which paper towel was strongest. Dev wanted to build a robot out of an old toaster.
They argued until neither of them had anything left to say. That was when they noticed the chocolate bar melting in the window.
"A solar oven," they said at the exact same time. It was the first thing they had ever agreed on.
They set up a workshop in Dev's garage. Maya made a six-week plan, and Dev collected boxes, foil and an old window.
Version one went together in an afternoon: a pizza box, foil flaps, black paper and plastic wrap on top.
It got hot, all right. The plastic wrap melted into goo, and so did the crayon they used to test it.
Version two got even hotter. A cardboard flap began to smoke, and Maya's dad came running with the hose.
They sat on the step with a soggy, scorched box. "Note: cardboard burns," Maya wrote, and Dev laughed so hard he snorted.
Version three had a wooden crate, the old window for a lid and mirror tiles Dev found at a yard sale.
That night a storm blew in. The wind tore a sheet of roof right off Dev's garage.
In the morning they helped Dev's grandpa fix the roof. Under its tarp, the oven didn't have a scratch.
Maya worked out the sun's angle, and Dev tilted every mirror to match. Teamwork, it turned out, worked.
The thermometer climbed and climbed. "It's working!" yelled Dev, and Maya did a dance on the driveway.
First test: cookies. Maya timed them to the second, and Dev waited with an oven mitt on each hand.
Second test: s'mores. The marshmallows puffed up like clouds, and Dev's little sister ate four.
Third test: a whole pizza. Maya wrote every number in her chart. Dev called it delicious data.
They built their display board on Maya's living room floor, with photos of every oven, even the burned one.
On fair morning, Dev's bike chain snapped halfway to school, with the oven in the trailer behind him.
Maya ran six blocks with her brother's wagon. They loaded the oven and raced to school together.
They made it with two minutes to spare. Maya explained the numbers, Dev explained the build, and the judges ate pizza.
They won honorable mention. Maya and Dev held the ribbon together, and neither one let go first.
On the bus home, Maya turned to a fresh page. "Next year," said Dev, "a wind turbine." Maya was already making a list.

pageTexts: Behind the kitchen wall of the Baker family's house lived a tiny mouse named Nutmeg.
Nutmeg had a matchbox bed, a button rug and a red knitted hat that kept her ears warm.
One snowy December day, the Bakers carried a big Christmas tree into the house.
That night, when everyone was asleep, Nutmeg crept out. "I will make Christmas too," she whispered.
She found a bowl of cranberries on the counter and rolled out one, two, three.
She threaded them on a long string and hung them along the shelf like a necklace.
She hung a shiny thimble from a hook. Ting! It was her very own Christmas bell.
Beside the cookie rack lay crumbs of gingerbread. Nutmeg had a wonderful idea.
She built a little gingerbread cottage with a frosting roof and a chocolate chip door.
She wrapped a walnut in a scrap of paper and tied it with a ribbon. A present!
From an old lost sock, she sewed a little stocking, stitch by tiny stitch.
Then Nutmeg tiptoed into the living room. The tree was so tall and sparkly!
She hopped onto the toy train. Choo choo! Around and around the tree she went.
She sat in a spoon and slid all the way down the banister. Wheee!
Bump! She landed at the bottom of the stairs. The cat opened one eye.
Nutmeg dived into a fluffy slipper and kept very, very still.
The cat yawned and went back to sleep. Phew! Nutmeg crept out of the slipper.
On Christmas Eve, she hung her little stocking by her mouse hole and put the walnut present beside it.
Then she climbed into her matchbox bed and fell fast asleep.
On Christmas morning, the Baker children ran into the kitchen. "Look! Who did all this?"
By the mouse hole they found a tiny stocking, a gingerbread cottage and a walnut wrapped with a bow.
"A mouse made Christmas for us," said the little boy. They put a crumb of cake in the stocking.
When Nutmeg peeked out, she found the cake in her stocking. She hugged it tight.
"Merry Christmas," whispered Nutmeg, and the Baker children waved back.

pageTexts: Thistle was a young reindeer with one crooked antler, and she dreamed of pulling the Christmas sleigh.
In November she lined up at the North Pole Flight School with all the other young reindeer.
Coach Birch looked at her bent antler. "Hmm," he said. "We'll see what you can do."
First came take-off practice on the ice runway. Thistle slipped and slid and spun around.
When she finally lifted off, her crooked antler tipped her sideways.
Crash! She landed in the snowman orchard and knocked the head off a snowman.
The elves put the snowman's head back on. "Try again tomorrow," they told her.
So Thistle practised every morning before anyone else was awake.
In loop class the big reindeer flew perfect circles over the elf village. Thistle flew a wobbly squiggle.
She ended up tangled in a string of Christmas lights between two rooftops.
Then came night flying. Each reindeer carried a lantern through the dark sky.
Thistle's lantern swung, and she lost the line behind a cloud.
A snowy owl flew beside her. "Follow the workshop lights," it hooted, and she found her way back.
At rooftop landing practice, Thistle skidded across the workshop roof and bumped the chimney.
In the harness relay against the older reindeer, Thistle pulled hard, but she finished last again.
That night Thistle lay in the barn. "Maybe a crooked antler can't pull a sleigh," she sighed.
The old sleigh driver, Grandmother Juniper, came by with a lantern. "Don't give up yet, little one," she said.
On Christmas Eve the sleigh was packed, but a howling blizzard swept over the North Pole.
The big reindeer tried to fly, but the wind pushed them back down. "We're grounded," said Coach Birch.
Thistle stepped into the storm. Her crooked antler caught the wind just right, and she rose straight up.
"Put her at the front!" cried Grandmother Juniper. Thistle led the team up through the snow.
Above the clouds the sky was calm and full of stars. They delivered every present before dawn.
When they landed back home, everyone cheered. Coach Birch gave Thistle a big nod.
The next morning a new banner hung over Thistle's stall, stitched with her name and one crooked antler.

pageTexts: Wilbur the penguin was the postmaster of the North Pole Post Office, and December was his busiest month.
Letters came by plane, dropped from the sky in big canvas bags.
Letters came by boat, handed up the icy dock by a walrus sailor.
And letters came by sled, piled higher than the dogs pulling them.
Wilbur sorted them into mountains: tall ones, short ones, and wobbly ones that fell right over.
Stamp, stamp, stamp! He stamped every single one.
Then the elves loaded the letters onto carts and rolled them off to the workshop.
On December 23, Wilbur was sweeping up when he spotted one letter hiding behind an old mailbag.
It was from a girl named Hana. "Please find my grandpa's lost music box," it said. "It played his favourite song."
The sleigh would leave tomorrow night. There was no time to lose!
Wilbur hitched up the dog sled, tucked the letter in his satchel and set off.
They raced across an iced-over lake, the ice creaking under the runners.
When it grew dark, they stopped at a lighthouse. The keeper lent Wilbur a lantern.
With the lantern swinging, Wilbur followed the path through the snowy forest.
At last he reached a tiny toy-repair shop at the edge of a sleepy village.
The old toymaker read the letter. "People bring me lost toys all year," she said. "Let's look."
They searched shelves of teddy bears, tin drums and wooden horses.
On the very top shelf, Wilbur found a little wooden music box with a dancer on the lid.
The toymaker fixed its spring and wound the key, and a sweet old song tinkled out.
Wilbur raced home all day on Christmas Eve, the music box wrapped safely in his scarf.
He reached the workshop just as the sleigh began to rise. "Wait!" he shouted. "One more!"
An elf leaned over the side and caught the music box. The sleigh flew off into the night.
On Christmas morning, Hana gave the music box to her grandpa. He wound it, and his old song played again.
A week later, a new letter arrived at the post office. It was a thank-you note, with a drawing of a penguin.

pageTexts: On Christmas Eve, Sofia and Max rolled the biggest snowball they had ever made.
They stacked one, two, three snowballs to make a snowman.
Sofia gave him a carrot nose. Max gave him pebble eyes and two stick arms.
Then they put an old captain's cap on his head. "You are Captain Carrot!" they cheered.
That night the children went to bed and waved goodnight to Captain Carrot.
When the house was dark, Captain Carrot blinked his pebble eyes and stretched. He was awake!
He hopped out of the gate and down the snowy street.
At the pond, he skated round and round on the ice. Swish, swoosh!
He found the Christmas market, full of little wooden stalls and twinkly lights.
He rode a painted horse on the carousel, up and down and round and round.
He sang with the carolers under the street lamp. La la la!
The baker had pies to deliver, so Captain Carrot helped carry them.
He left a warm pie on every doorstep on the street.
Up in the tower, he pulled the rope and rang the big bell. Dong, dong!
At the station, he waved at the late train as it puffed by. Toot toot!
He zoomed down the big hill on a tea tray. Wheee!
Then he sat under the big town tree and looked up at the shining star.
The baker wrapped a warm new scarf around his neck. "Thank you for helping," she said.
A stall keeper gave him a candy cane, the biggest one in the whole market.
The sky began to turn pink. "Time to go home!" said Captain Carrot, and he hurried back.
He hopped back into the yard, stood very still, and closed his pebble eyes.
On Christmas morning, Sofia and Max woke up and ran outside in their pajamas and boots.
Captain Carrot had a new scarf and a candy cane! And there were snowy footprints by the gate.
"Merry Christmas, Captain Carrot!" they said. And they were sure he winked.

The old farm pickup truck driving through a snowy town with the big tree tied in the back and a stack of wreaths beside it.
A hospital playroom where children in pajamas, one in a wheelchair, hang paper stars and ornaments on the big tree with Hattie's help.

pageTexts: Every December, Hattie helped Grandpa at Pine Hollow, the family Christmas tree farm.
One week before Christmas, Grandpa slipped on the icy barn steps.
His arm was broken. "You know this farm better than anyone," he said, and handed Hattie the keys.
At dawn the next day, Hattie pulled on her work gloves. The first cars were already pulling in.
She walked families through the rows and tied a tag to every tree they chose.
She drove the tractor and pulled the hay wagon full of families up and down the hill.
"Will it fit in our living room?" a dad asked. Hattie measured it with the tall pole.
She tied trees to car roofs, pulling the twine tight with the knot Grandpa had taught her.
She kept the bonfire burning so people could warm their hands and toast marshmallows.
At the cocoa stand, she poured mug after mug, with a candy cane in each.
That night she fell asleep at the kitchen table. Grandpa laid a quilt over her with his good arm.
On the third day, a little boy came running. "Our dog Pepper ran into the trees!"
Hattie followed the paw prints deep into the oldest pines.
She found Pepper tangled in a roll of old tree netting, shivering but safe.
She carried Pepper back, and the boy hugged him so hard his hat fell off.
Then the tree baler jammed, with a big fir stuck halfway through and a line of customers waiting.
Grandpa couldn't use his arm, so he talked her through the repair while she worked with the wrench.
With one last turn, the gear clicked into place, and the tree slid out wrapped and ready.
In the evenings she made wreaths in the barn, with pine branches, pinecones and red bows.
On Christmas Eve, Hattie and Grandpa picked the finest tree on the farm. It was not for sale.
They drove it to the children's hospital in town as a gift, with a stack of wreaths beside it.
The children helped decorate it, hanging paper stars and ornaments on every branch.
Back home, there was one small tree left on the hill. They cut it last, just for themselves.
That night their own tree glowed in the farmhouse window. "Best week ever," said Grandpa.

pages.intro: An ocean adventure story coloring book takes kids from the beach to the deep sea, with coral reefs, kelp forests and shipwrecks to color along the way. pageTexts: Bubbles was a baby seahorse. She lived on the coral reef with her dad.
One day a big current came. Whoosh! It pulled Bubbles away.
Bubbles looked around. She could not see her dad anywhere.
"Have you seen my dad?" Bubbles asked a clownfish.
"Not today," said the clownfish. "Ask the turtle on the ledge."
The sea turtle was fast asleep. Bubbles gave his shell a tap.
"Mmm, try past the sand," yawned the turtle.
Past the sand was a pufferfish. "Go away!" he puffed.
Then he felt sorry. "Ask the eel in the rocks," he said.
The moray eel opened his big mouth. "Ask the shrimp," he said.
The shrimp were busy cleaning a grouper's teeth.
"Go that way," they said, and pointed with their feelers.
That way was an octopus who could change her stripes to spots!
"Hold on," said the octopus, and lifted Bubbles over the wall.
Crunch, crunch! A parrotfish was eating coral.
"I make sand," said the parrotfish. "Follow it to the ray."
The ray let Bubbles ride along. Swoosh, over the sand!
"Your dad likes the seagrass," said the ray. "It is just there."
Bubbles was very tired. But she did not give up.
She came to the seagrass meadow. The grass was so tall!
Bubbles swam between the blades. "Dad? Dad!"
And there was Dad, holding onto the grass, waiting for her.
Bubbles curled her tail around his. "I found you!"
All her new friends came to say hello. Bubbles was home.

arguments.description: Juno, a humpback whale calf with one white flipper, is born in a warm lagoon. In spring she and her mother swim north thousands of miles to the cold feeding grounds. On the way Juno practices breaching, races spinner dolphins, rests over a coral bank, passes a container ship, hides from orcas behind her mother, sees sea lions on a buoy, swims under a fishing boat, hears other whales singing and crosses the open ocean in a storm. In the cold waters she sees icebergs and krill, and joins the adults blowing bubble nets to feed. 24 pages.

pageTexts: Juno was born in a warm blue lagoon. Her mother pushed her up gently for her very first breath.
Juno had one white flipper. She liked to rest under her mother's big flipper and drink milk.
Every day she practised jumping. Her first breach was more of a flop, but she was proud.
When spring came, her mother said, "Now we swim north, all the way to the cold seas."
Spinner dolphins joined them on the first day. They spun in the air and dared Juno to race.
At night they rested over a coral bank, where turtles and little fish swam below.
Juno learned to breathe in rhythm with her mother: swim, swim, up, puff.
A giant ship rumbled past. "Ships are loud," said her mother. "We stay well away."
One morning, tall black fins appeared. Orcas! Juno hid beneath her mother.
Her mother lifted her mighty tail and stood her ground. The orcas swam away.
Farther north, sea lions barked at Juno from a buoy. She barked a bubble right back.
They swam deep under a fishing boat. "Never play near the nets," her mother warned.
Along the coast was a kelp forest, where a sea otter cracked open his lunch.
Juno poked her head straight up to look at the land. A lighthouse looked back.
That evening, she heard a strange, beautiful sound. Far away, other whales were singing.
Juno tried to sing too. It came out squeaky, but her mother said it was perfect.
Then a storm came. The waves were as tall as hills, but Juno stayed close and kept swimming.
When the storm was over, a rainbow stretched across the sky, and Juno slapped the water for joy.
Day after day they crossed the open ocean. Flying fish skipped ahead like a welcome.
At last the water turned icy. Juno saw her first iceberg, with a puffin on top.
The sea was full of krill, tiny shrimp by the million. This was why they had come!
The grown whales swam in a circle and blew a net of bubbles to round up the krill.
Juno blew bubbles too. Then everyone rose up together, mouths wide, for a giant gulp.
Full and happy, Juno rested beside her mother. She had swum the whole way north.

prompts.name: Finn's message in a bottle
prompts.brief: Finn, eight, in a striped life jacket, finds a bottle on the beach with a hand-drawn picture map inside. He and his grandpa sail their small boat, the Pelican, to follow it. The last mark leads to a tin of her childhood treasures buried under a palm. Finn adds his own drawing and they bury it again. 24 pages.

pageTexts: Finn was hunting for shells at low tide when he saw something shining in the sand. A bottle!
Inside was a rolled-up paper. "Grandpa!" Finn shouted. "Come and look!"
It was a map with no words, just little pictures joined by a dotted line. "Let's follow it," said Grandpa.
The next morning they packed a picnic and got the Pelican ready to sail.
Out of the harbor they went, with the wind in the sail and the map in Finn's hand.
The first picture was a lighthouse. And there it was, on a rocky little island!
From the top, Finn could see far out to sea. "I see a sandbar next!"
The sandbar was covered in seals. One curious pup came to say hello.
Finn checked the map. The next picture was a bird in a tree.
They rowed into a mangrove, where the roots twisted like fingers into the water.
High in the branches was a heron on her nest. "Bird in a tree," Finn whispered.
Over lunch, Grandpa tapped the map. "A fish next. Time to get wet."
Finn snorkeled over the reef. Fish of every shape swam around him.
A sea turtle glided by, and a giant clam opened its wavy shell.
The next picture was a boat. In a quiet cove lay an old shipwreck.
Inside, carved into a beam, was a little star, just like the one on the map.
The dotted line ended at a village. "Someone here must know this map," said Grandpa.
Finn showed the map to an old woman mending her nets on the porch.
Her eyes went wide. "I drew this when I was a girl," she said, "seventy years ago!"
She showed them her old notebook. The drawings looked just the same.
"The last picture is my secret palm tree," she said. "Let's go and see."
Finn dug and dug under the palm. Clink! His shovel hit a rusty tin.
Inside were her childhood treasures. She laughed and held up her little wooden boat.
Finn added a drawing of his own, and they buried the tin again for someone new to find.

prompts.name: Amaya's dive to the ocean floor
prompts.brief: Amaya, twelve, with a braid tucked into a ship's cap, joins her mother's research crew for a dive in the submersible Kestrel. They sink through the zones: the sunlit zone with tuna and jellyfish, the twilight zone with lanternfish and a giant squid's eye in the dark, the midnight zone with an anglerfish and a vampire squid, then the abyss with sea pigs and glass sponges. At the bottom they reach a hydrothermal vent with tube worms and white crabs, and Amaya spots a sea cucumber no one has seen before. Back on deck, the scientists name the new species after her. 24 pages.
prompts.why: Older ocean fans and science teachers get a 24-page dive through every ocean zone with real deep-sea animals at each depth.

arguments.title: Down to the Abyss
arguments.description: Amaya, twelve, with a braid tucked into a ship's cap, joins her mother's research crew for a dive in the submersible Kestrel. pages: A research ship on a calm sea at dawn, its crane swinging the round submersible Kestrel over the side, Amaya at the rail with her sketchbook under one arm.
Amaya climbing down the hatch on top of the Kestrel, her mother already inside, deck crew in hard hats and life vests holding the cables.
Inside the Kestrel: three seats facing a big round window, screens and dials, a pilot at the joystick and Amaya pressing her hands to the glass.
The Kestrel splashing down into the waves, two divers in wetsuits unhooking it from the crane line, the ship's hull towering beside it.
The sunlit zone through the dome window: a school of fast tuna streaking past, beams of sunlight slanting down through the water.
Moon jellyfish drifting past the Kestrel's window with long trailing arms, a sea turtle far off, the sunbeams fading above.
The twilight zone: a school of small lanternfish dotted with rows of glowing spots, swimming in the dim water around the submersible's lamps.
A giant squid's enormous eye at the very edge of the Kestrel's lamplight, long tentacles trailing into the dark, Amaya gasping at the window.
Amaya inside the cabin sketching a hatchetfish in her book, her mother writing notes beside her, a depth gauge and a thermos on the panel.
The midnight zone: an anglerfish with a glowing lure dangling in front of its wide, toothy mouth, lit up by the submersible's lamps.

A gulper eel with a huge balloon-like mouth and a long whip tail, a few comb jellies with rippling stripes drifting nearby.
A small dumbo octopus flapping its ear-like fins as it hovers in the dark water in front of the Kestrel's lamps.
The abyss: the Kestrel's lights shining on a soft muddy seafloor where a group of sea pigs walk along on tiny tube feet.
Tall glass sponges shaped like lacy vases on the seafloor, a brittle star curled on one, a tripod fish standing on its long fin spikes.
One of the Kestrel's robot arms pushing a clear tube into the mud to take a sample, Amaya and her mother working the controls together.
A hydrothermal vent: a tall rocky black chimney on the seafloor puffing thick clouds of hot mineral smoke into the water.
Thick bundles of giant tube worms with feathery tips around the vent, white crabs crawling over the rocks between them.
A strange see-through sea cucumber with frilly lace fins floating above the seafloor, Amaya pointing at it through the dome window.
The robot arm gently scooping the new sea cucumber into a clear collection box, the pilot steering, Amaya watching with both hands clasped.
The Kestrel rising toward the surface after dropping its ballast weights, a trail of bubbles streaming up from it in the dark water.
The Kestrel bobbing at the surface at sunset, divers reattaching the crane line, the research ship waiting close by.
Scientists in the ship's lab crowding around a glass tank holding the sea cucumber, Amaya at the front with her sketchbook open.
The crew clapping as a scientist pins Amaya's drawing of the new sea cucumber on the lab wall, her mother hugging her from the side.
pageTexts: At dawn the crane lifted the Kestrel over the side of the ship. Amaya had waited her whole life for this dive.
Her mother was the lead scientist, and today Amaya was part of the crew. She climbed down the hatch and the lid sealed shut above her.
Inside, there were three seats, a hundred dials and one big round window. Amaya pressed her hands against the cold glass.
With a splash the Kestrel hit the water. The divers unhooked the line, and they began to sink.
The first part of the ocean is the sunlit zone. Tuna flashed past like silver arrows in the sunbeams.
Moon jellyfish drifted by. Above them, the light was already fading from blue to grey.
At two hundred meters they entered the twilight zone. Lanternfish twinkled like a sky full of stars.
Then something huge moved at the edge of the lights: the eye of a giant squid, bigger than a dinner plate. It blinked, and was gone.
Amaya sketched every animal she saw. Her mother logged the depth: five hundred meters and falling.
Below a thousand meters, no sunlight ever reaches. In the midnight zone, an anglerfish dangled its glowing lure.
A vampire squid flipped its arms over its head like a cloak. It looked fierce, but it was only shy.
A gulper eel opened a mouth far too big for its body. Comb jellies rippled with light around it.
Then came Amaya's favorite: a tiny dumbo octopus, flapping its fins like little ears.
After three hours they reached the abyss, four thousand meters down. Sea pigs plodded across the mud.
Glass sponges stood like delicate vases, and a tripod fish waited patiently on its three long fins.
"Your turn," said her mother. Amaya steered the robot arm and took her first mud sample.
Farther on, the water grew warm. Ahead stood a hydrothermal vent, puffing black smoke from inside the Earth.
Giant tube worms crowded around it, and white crabs scuttled between them. Life, even here, in the dark.
Then Amaya saw something no one on board had seen before: a see-through sea cucumber with frilly fins.
Very gently, the robot arm guided it into a collection box. Amaya held her breath the whole time.
The Kestrel dropped its weights and began the long climb back toward the light.
When they reached the surface, the sun was setting. The divers were waiting to bring them home.
In the lab, the scientists crowded around the tank. Nobody could find the creature in any book.
"Every new species needs a name," said her mother. They named it after Amaya, and pinned her drawing on the wall.

prompts.name: Pearl the hermit crab's new shell
prompts.brief: Pearl, a hermit crab with striped legs and one big claw, has grown too big for her snail shell. She sets off across the tide pools to find a new home. She tries a bottle cap, a teacup washed up on the sand, a toy bucket, a coconut, an old boot, a sea urchin's empty shell and a jar, and every one is too big, too small, too heavy or too leaky. She asks a starfish, a sea anemone, a gull and a lobster for help. At the edge of the rocks she finds a whelk shell that fits just right, and she gives her old shell to a smaller crab. 24 pages.

pageTexts: Pearl the hermit crab had a problem. Her shell was too small!
She squeezed and she squished. But her big claw would not fit inside.
"I need a new home," said Pearl, and off she went.
She found a bottle cap. Too small!
She found a teacup. Too big! Pearl slid all around.
She found a toy bucket. Way too big!
"Can you help me?" she asked a starfish. "Keep looking," said the starfish.
She found a coconut. Too heavy! It would not move.
She found an old boot. Too leaky! Drip, drip, drip.
"Can you help me?" she asked a sea anemone. "Not me," it said, and waved.
She found a sea urchin shell. Too many holes!
"Can you help me?" she asked a gull. "Squawk!" said the gull.
She found a jar. Too slippery! And everyone could see in.
Pearl sat down. "Nothing is right," she said with a sigh.
Then she met a big lobster. "Can you help me?" she asked.
"Go to the edge of the rocks," said the lobster.
So Pearl walked and walked to the very edge of the rocks.
And there it was: a tall, pointy shell.
She peeked inside. Nobody home!
Quick as a wink, Pearl wiggled in.
It fit just right! Pearl did a happy dance.
Then she saw a tiny crab with no shell at all.
"Here," said Pearl. "You can have my old one."
Now they both had homes, and they waved to all their friends.

pages.title: Bedtime Story Prompts for Kids: AI Picture Book Ideas
pages.metaDescription: Three 24-page bedtime story prompts written page by page: a hedgehog in a moonflower garden, ten sheep who won't sleep and a boy who borrows the moon.
pages.intro: A good bedtime story book slows down as it goes, until the last page is almost a whisper. These three 24-page picture books are for parents who want a bedtime story of their own and KDP sellers building a cozy list: a hedgehog who stays up for the last moonflower, a girl who settles ten restless sheep while counting to ten, and a boy afraid of the dark who borrows the moon. Each is written out page by page, with the words and the picture for every page, so you can paste one page at a time into ChatGPT, Gemini or any AI image tool.
tips: End every bedtime story with the hero asleep or nearly asleep; the book should land where the child is.
Soft styles like colored pencil or paper cut-out suit bedtime better than bold comic looks.
KDP paperbacks need at least 24 pages, so each book here is 24; for home printing you can trim a few middle pages down to 16.

prompts.name: Bramble and the moonflowers
prompts.brief: A 24-page bedtime story. Every night after the village falls asleep, Mrs. Fernsby, a tall old badger in a patched blue apron, waters the moonflowers that open only in the dark. Tonight her helper Bramble, a sleepy hedgehog with a tiny lantern, wants to stay up to see the very last one bloom. He yawns through every chore: the well, the weeds, a snail moved to the lettuce. The last flower opens just for him. Bramble curls up among the glowing petals, and Mrs. Fernsby carries him home to bed. Hushed, slow and gentle.
prompts.why: Parents get a quiet, beautifully lit story that slows toward sleep, the exact mood a bedtime book has to hold.

Bramble lying on his tummy in the soft grass beside the last closed moonflower bud, chin in his paws, watching it very closely, his lantern set beside him.
Bramble's lantern burning low and dim as his head sinks onto his paws, the last bud still shut, a single firefly resting on the bud's tip.
Bramble with his nose almost touching the closed bud, whispering, his eyes nearly shut, a dewdrop hanging from a leaf beside him.
The last moonflower slowly unfolding its petals right in front of Bramble, the brightest glow in the garden, sparkles of silver light floating up into the dark.
Close-up of Bramble's small face lit silver by the glowing open flower, his eyes shining and a tiny sleepy smile, his paws clasped together.
Bramble curled up in a little ball inside the wide glowing petals of the last moonflower, his lantern gone out beside the stem, a moth resting on a leaf.
Mrs. Fernsby bending over the last moonflower and finding Bramble fast asleep inside it, her paw on her heart, her watering can set down on the path.
Mrs. Fernsby walking home along the garden path carrying the sleeping Bramble in the crook of one arm and his lantern in her other paw, the glowing garden behind her.
Bramble fast asleep in a little basket bed with a patchwork quilt by a round cottage window, the moonflower garden glowing silver outside, Mrs. Fernsby blowing out a candle.
pageTexts: When the last light in the village goes out, Mrs. Fernsby puts on her patched blue apron. It is time to tend the night garden.
Bramble trots behind her with his tiny lantern. "Tonight I'm staying up," he says, and then he yawns.
The garden gate creaks open. Row after row of moonflowers wait in the dark, every bud shut tight.
"Moonflowers open only in the dark," says Mrs. Fernsby. "And the very last one waits for the deepest part of the night."
"Then I will see the very last one," says Bramble. He stands up tall to show how awake he is.
First they fill the watering can at the old stone well. Bramble holds it steady. His eyes close, just for a moment.
Splish, splash, down the long rows. Bramble lights the way, and his lantern swings slow and low.
Next come the weeds, one little tug at a time. Bramble yawns so wide that his whiskers wobble.
A snail is nibbling a moonflower leaf. Bramble carries it, very gently, to the lettuce patch instead.
Then, with a tiny sigh, the first moonflower opens. It glows like a little moon of its own.
One by one more flowers open. Soft white moths come to visit, quiet as whispers.
Bramble sits down on a flowerpot to rest. Only for a moment, he tells himself.
Mrs. Fernsby hums an old, slow tune as she ties up the tallest stems. Hum, hum, goes the night.
Hoo, hoo, says the owl in the apple tree. Even the owl sounds sleepy tonight.
Now the whole garden shines silver. All the moonflowers are open, all but one.
Bramble lies down beside the last bud to watch. He will not miss it. Not this one.
His lantern burns low. His head sinks lower. The last bud stays shut tight.
"Please," Bramble whispers, very softly. "I stayed up just for you."
And slowly, slowly, the very last moonflower opens, just for him.
It is the brightest, softest flower of all. Bramble smiles the sleepiest smile.
He curls up among the glowing petals. They are warm, and they smell like sweet milk.
Mrs. Fernsby finds him there, fast asleep. "You saw it," she whispers. "You stayed up after all."
She carries him home past the sleeping rows, the garden glowing softly behind them.
She tucks him into bed and blows out the candle. Outside, the moonflowers keep watch. Goodnight, Bramble.

prompts.name: Ten sheep who would not sleep
prompts.brief: A 24-page counting bedtime story. Pim, a little girl in yellow rain boots and a nightgown, can't fall asleep, so she tries counting sheep. But her ten sheep won't jump the fence: Clover wants a snack, Wooly lost her bell, the twins want one more game of tag, Hiccup has hiccups, Tuft is cold, Mumble wants a story, Little Lou wants a song, Puff's bed is lumpy and Big Bertha is scared of the dark. Pim helps each one settle, counting up to ten, until all ten snore in a woolly pile. Then Pim climbs onto the softest sheep and falls asleep too.
prompts.why: Toddlers learn to count to ten inside a bedtime routine, and short lettered pages suit parents printing at home.

Pim yawning a huge yawn and climbing onto Big Bertha's soft woolly back, her yellow rain boots dangling, the other sheep asleep around her.
Pim fast asleep back in her own bed, smiling, hugging a small toy sheep, her yellow rain boots by the bed and moonlight on the floor.
pageTexts: Pim is not sleepy. Not one bit. The clock goes tick, tock, tick.
"I know," says Pim. "I'll count sheep!" She shuts her eyes tight.
There is the meadow. There is the fence. And there are ten sheep, all in a row.
"Jump!" says Pim. But not one sheep jumps. Not even a little hop.
"I'm hungry," says Clover. So Pim picks her a snack of sweet green clover.
Crunch, munch, yawn. Clover curls up and closes her eyes. One!
"I lost my bell," says Wooly. "I can't sleep without my bell."
Pim finds it in the daisies, ting-a-ling. Wooly snuggles down. Two!
"One more game of tag!" shout the twins, Dot and Dash. Round and round they run.
Tag, you're it, and tag, you're it! The twins flop down, puffing and giggling. Three, four!
"Hic!" says Hiccup. "Hic! I can't stop!" Each hic makes her bounce.
Pim gives her slow, slow sips of water. The hiccups float away. Five!
"Brrr," says Tuft. "The night is too chilly for me."
Pim tucks a little quilt around her, snug as a bun. Six!
"I need a story," mumbles Mumble. "Just a short one, please."
Pim tells the shortest story ever: once upon a time, a sheep fell asleep. The end. Seven!
"Sing me a song?" asks Little Lou, the smallest sheep of all.
Pim sings la-la-lullaby, soft and low. Little Lou is asleep before the end. Eight!
Puff turns round and round. "My bed is too lumpy!" Pim fluffs a pile of soft hay. Nine!
But Big Bertha is hiding behind the fence. "I'm scared of the dark," she whispers.
"Look," says Pim. "The moon is our night-light, and the stars are on too." Big Bertha looks up.
Big Bertha sighs and settles down with the others. Ten! Ten sheep, snoring in a woolly pile.
Pim yawns the biggest yawn of all. She climbs onto Big Bertha, the softest sheep.
Snore, snore, goes the meadow. And Pim? Pim is fast asleep too. Goodnight.

prompts.name: The boy who borrowed the moon
prompts.brief: A 24-page bedtime story about fear of the dark. Arlo, a boy with messy red hair who wears his blanket as a cape, is scared of the shadows in his room. One night he climbs a very tall ladder and borrows the moon as his night-light. But without the moon the owl can't hunt, the tide forgets to come in, the fireflies get lost and a fox cub can't find its way home. Arlo sees the night needs its moon more than he does. He carries it back up the ladder, and from then on the moon slips a silver beam through his window every night to keep him company.
prompts.why: Early readers who fear the dark get a story that answers the fear with wonder, a classic shape for a KDP bedtime title.

The owl swooping over a silver moonlit field with its wings spread wide, the moon shining behind it and a small mouse hiding under a leaf.
Arlo climbing back into his bed in his blanket cape, looking a little nervous at the dark corners of his room, the ladder leaning outside his window.

pageTexts: Arlo was not afraid of spiders, or thunder, or big dogs. But he was very afraid of the dark.
At night his coat on the hook looked like a bear. His chair looked like it might creep across the floor.
One night he looked out of his window at the moon, so round and bright. And Arlo had an idea.
He tiptoed into the garden and pulled the longest ladder out of the shed.
Up he climbed, past the chimneys, past the treetops, past the sleepy clouds.
"Excuse me, Moon," said Arlo. "May I borrow you, just for tonight? I need a night-light."
The moon was surprised, but it said yes. Arlo tucked it under his arm and climbed carefully down.
He set the moon on his shelf. His whole room glowed silver, and there were no bears and no monsters at all.
But outside, the sky was black. Without the moon, the owl could not see a thing in the fields below.
Down by the harbour, the tide forgot to come in. The little boats sat stuck on the sand.
In the meadow, the fireflies got lost. They bumped into grass, and into each other, and into a very cross hedgehog.
A fox cub could not find the path home. Which way? Which way? It was much too dark to tell.
Tap, tap, tap. Arlo woke to find the owl at his window. "Where has the moon gone?" it hooted.
Arlo looked at the moon on his shelf. His cheeks went hot. "I borrowed it," he said in a small voice.
He carried the moon outside to see. There were the boats, stuck on the sand, waiting for the sea.
In the meadow, the lost fireflies blinked at him, and the fox cub was still looking for its way home.
Arlo hugged the moon tight. Then he understood. The night needed its moon more than he did.
So up the ladder he went again. The moon was heavy, and his arms were tired, but Arlo did not stop.
At the very top, he lifted the moon back into its place in the sky. "Thank you for lending me your light," he said.
At once, the tide rushed in and lifted the boats. The fireflies found their way, and the fox cub ran home.
The owl swooped happily over the fields. The night was itself again.
Arlo climbed back into bed. The corners of his room were dark again, and he felt a little bit scared.
Then a long silver moonbeam slipped through his window and lay across his blanket, soft and bright.
From then on, every night, the moon sent Arlo a moonbeam to keep him company. And Arlo was never afraid of the dark again.

pages.title: Friendship Story Prompts for Kids' Picture Books
pages.metaDescription: Three 24-page friendship picture book prompts, written page by page: a tortoise and a duckling, a lonely robot and two balcony pen pals.
pages.intro: These friendship picture books are for children aged 3 to 9 and the parents, teachers and KDP sellers who read with them: two characters who don't fit together, a problem, and the moment they realise they need each other. A slow tortoise and a speedy duckling find their way home through a flood, a lonely clock-shop robot learns a friend can't be built, and two children without a shared language trade drawings across a street. Each book is written out page by page, with the words and the picture for all 24 pages, so you can paste one page at a time into ChatGPT, Gemini or any AI image tool.
tips: Make the two friends opposites (slow and fast, quiet and loud) so the story has built-in tension.
Let the friendship be tested once before the happy ending; it makes the ending earned.
Give each friend one fixed visual trait so they look the same on every page.

prompts.name: Pebble the tortoise and Dabble the duckling
prompts.brief: A 24-page picture book. Pebble, a careful tortoise with a moss-green shell, and Dabble, a splashy yellow duckling with one wonky feather, disagree about everything: Pebble likes slow walks and quiet, Dabble likes racing and quacking. When a storm floods the meadow, Dabble can swim but can't find the way home, and Pebble knows every path but can't swim. Pebble rides on Dabble's back and gives directions while she paddles past the fence post, the oak tree and the bridge. They get home together under a rainbow and decide being different is the best part.
prompts.why: Preschoolers see two opposite friends solve a problem together, a gentle lesson parents and teachers read again and again.

pageTexts: Pebble the tortoise lived at the edge of a sunny meadow. He liked to take things slowly.
Dabble the duckling lived by the pond. She liked to do everything fast!
One morning, Dabble zoomed around a bush and bumped right into Pebble. Bump! "Oops!" said Dabble.
"Let's be friends!" said Dabble. "Let's race to the big oak tree!"
Dabble raced. Pebble walked. By the time Pebble got there, Dabble was fast asleep.
"Let's sing loud songs!" quacked Dabble. "I like quiet," said Pebble.
Pebble liked to munch dandelions. Dabble liked to gobble pondweed.
Pebble liked to nap in the warm sun. Dabble could not sit still for one minute.
"We are too different to be friends," sighed Pebble. Dabble's wonky feather drooped.
That afternoon, big dark clouds rolled over the meadow. Whoosh went the wind.
Rain poured down. Drip, drop, splash! The meadow began to fill with water.
Dabble swam round and round. The water had covered every path. Which way was home?
On a little hill, Pebble sat on a rock. He knew every path in the meadow, but he could not swim.
"Pebble!" called Dabble. She paddled as fast as she could toward the hill.
"I can swim, but I am lost," said Dabble. "I know the way, but I can't swim," said Pebble.
Then Dabble had an idea. "Climb on my back!"
"Left at the old fence post!" said Pebble. Dabble paddled left.
"Now straight past the big oak tree!" Dabble paddled and paddled.
"Under the little bridge, then right at the bulrushes!" The rain began to stop.
At last they saw home: Pebble's cozy burrow and Dabble's nest, high and dry on the bank.
The sun came out, and a rainbow stretched over the meadow.
"You were fast when we needed fast," said Pebble. "And you were careful when we needed careful," said Dabble.
The next day, they took a slow walk and a quick swim. Then they sang a very quiet song together.
Pebble and Dabble were as different as can be. And that was the best part.

prompts.name: Cog the clock-shop robot
prompts.brief: A 24-page picture book. Cog, a small rusty robot with one wobbly wheel and a lightbulb antenna, lives alone in a dusty clock-repair shop after the old clockmaker retires. He builds friends from springs and gears: a teapot dog, a pocket-watch bird, a toaster with a smile. None of them can talk back. Then Nell, a girl with a red toolbox and orange overalls, comes in looking for spare parts. She fixes Cog's wheel; he helps her finish her go-kart and fixes its steering. Cog learns a friend isn't something you build. It's someone who listens and helps.
prompts.why: Kids aged 6-9 love robots, and the story's clear idea of friendship gives parents and teachers something to discuss.
